cd.headline: DR Congo signs US$41 million contract for Ngandajika agro-industrial park
cd.dek: Construction is scheduled to start in January 2027, while separate private investment is being assessed for processing plants and logistics facilities.
paragraphs: The Democratic Republic of Congo has signed a US$41 million contract to build the Ngandajika agro-industrial park in Lomami province, with construction scheduled to start in January 2027. A Chinese company will do the work, Bruno Miteyo Nyenge, head of the president’s Civil Household, said in a message reported by 7sur7.cd.

The park covers 534 hectares, including 159 hectares for livestock farming, 51 for industrial activity and 32 for logistics, according to African Development Bank procurement documents. Planned facilities include slaughterhouses, a laboratory and an agricultural services centre. The contractor’s identity and the contract’s completion deadline have not been disclosed.

A separate 2026 government-AfDB financing agreement worth about US$155 million covers transport links. The AfDB extended the deadline for bids on two road contracts, covering 125 kilometres in total, from December 4 to December 18, 2026. Each road project is expected to take 30 months.

tz.headline: Tanzania High Court orders immediate end to X restrictions
tz.dek: The judges ruled that blocking the platform exceeded regulators’ powers and violated users’ constitutional rights.
paragraphs: Tanzania’s High Court has ordered the government to immediately lift restrictions on X, formerly Twitter, ruling that regulators lacked authority to block the entire platform. The judgment, dated November 24, 2026, concerns restrictions imposed in May 2025.

The court said powers to remove prohibited content did not authorise a nationwide block, and rejected public safety, health and morality as grounds without a law permitting such a measure. It directed the government, the communications regulator and the attorney general to end blocks, throttling and other restrictions, ensuring access for the petitioners and the public.

The ruling still allows regulators to remove or block specific content that is prohibited under applicable law. The court made no costs order because the case was a public-interest constitutional petition.

tz.headline: Tanzania secures 4.7 billion US dollars in climate investment opportunities
tz.dek: Of the commitments, the African Development Bank approved 54m US dollars for 70,000 electric stoves for schools and health facilities.
paragraphs: Commitments worth 4.7 billion US dollars were secured by Tanzania at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Türkiye from November 9 to 22, 2026, to fund projects addressing climate change impacts. Minister of State in the Vice-President's Office for Union and Environment Hamad Masauni announced the figure in Dar es Salaam on November 27.

Across 12 funding areas, the commitments are spread, and the government will track their implementation to ensure the money is used as intended. Procurement of 70,000 modern electric cooking stoves for schools and health facilities was approved at 54m US dollars by the African Development Bank. Separately, the United Kingdom's aid agency pledged two million pounds for clean cooking energy and two million pounds for renewable energy.

Tanzania was also placed in an investment programme worth more than 4 billion US dollars for clean cooking energy. About one million people are expected to benefit from the electric stoves, paid for in instalments on their electricity bills.

tz.headline: Beginnings Fund pledges $85 million for Tanzania maternal care
tz.dek: The five-year partnership allocates $75.4 million to mainland Tanzania and $9.6 million to Zanzibar, with care for women and newborns as its target.
paragraphs: Tanzania will receive US$85 million over five years from the Beginnings Fund to improve maternal and newborn care, announced on November 26 at a national health conference in Dar es Salaam. President Samia Suluhu Hassan used the same event to call for stronger regional accountability to prevent childbirth deaths and bring services to women wherever they live.

Fund chief executive Alice Kang’ethe said US$75.4 million would go to mainland Tanzania and US$9.6 million to Zanzibar. The mainland programme will support 210 facilities, aiming to reach about 7.3 million women and newborns, with money directed to health workers, equipment, medicines and delivery systems. The Health Ministry and the Prime Minister’s Office will lead implementation.

Alongside the partnership, a mortality report put maternal deaths in 2024/25 at 76 per 100,000 live births, Samia said. Mortality among newborns stood at 17 per 1,000 live births, and among children under five at 28 per 1,000. The same event launched a reproductive and child health plan covering 2026 to 2030.

tz.headline: Dodoma and Aga Khan Foundation launch gender-violence campaign with income programme
tz.dek: The Tuinuke Pamoja project pairs community education on gender-based violence with household income activities across seven districts, delivered through 105 local groups.
paragraphs: Dodoma's regional government has joined the Aga Khan Foundation (AKF) in a campaign against gender-based violence that pairs education with economic empowerment. The work runs under the Tuinuke Pamoja project, which the Irish embassy in Tanzania funds and AKF carries out across seven districts.

Onorata Rwegasira, a community development officer with the regional secretariat, said the partners are encouraging couples to work together on income-generating activities, arguing that a better household economy can ease tension at home. Project officer Agnes Nkuba said AKF works through 105 groups across Dodoma's councils, using a publicity vehicle, open discussions, religious and traditional leaders and community groups to reach residents.

The campaign was launched on 25 November. Asha Nyoni, coordinator of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence at the Ministry of Community Development, Gender, Women and Special Groups, said the government wants to work with development partners, including AKF, to end all forms of gender-based violence.

tz.headline: JKCI seeks 25 billion/- for cardiac care at December 4 gala
tz.dek: The institute plans to fund heart surgery, build a House of Hope and buy diagnostic equipment for school screening programmes.
paragraphs: Tanzania’s Jakaya Kikwete Cardiac Institute (JKCI) and the Heart Team Africa Foundation are organising a fundraising gala for December 4 at Malaika Beach Resort in Mwanza Region. JKCI has asked President Samia Suluhu Hassan to attend as guest of honour. The organisers aim to raise 25 billion/- for cardiac healthcare services over five years.

JKCI Executive Director Dr Peter Kisenge said the money would help children from low-income families obtain treatment and surgery. The plans include a fund for heart operations, a House of Hope, diagnostic equipment for school screening and support for research. Kisenge said about 1,500 children need heart surgery, which costs between 10m/- and 30m/- per operation.

The government covers more than 70% of treatment costs, Kisenge said. JKCI performs minimally invasive heart surgery on about 400 children and 400 adults each year; more than 3,000 patients receive minimally invasive procedures. The institute says 97% of such surgeries are now performed in Tanzania.

ma.headline: Morocco enters cereal season with dams 64% full as El Niño risk builds
ma.dek: Reservoirs held 9.3 billion cubic meters by Nov. 10, but rainfall remained 36% below the 30-year average.
paragraphs: Morocco began planting winter wheat and barley in early November with dam reserves at 9.3 billion cubic meters, or 64% of capacity, a parliamentary report said. The country is monitoring a developing El Niño, but the meteorological agency says its direct effect on Morocco’s winter weather is expected to be limited.

Morocco received 43 millimeters of rain by Nov. 10, 183% more than in the same period a year earlier but 36% below the 30-year average of 68 millimeters. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said reservoirs were nearly 66% full in early November, compared with about 30% a year earlier. It estimated 2026 cereal production at 9 million tonnes, nearly 70% above the five-year average and almost double 2025 output.

The FAO said most of Morocco’s cereal production is rainfed, making rainfall through the growing season important. International forecasts point to El Niño peaking around December 2026 and continuing through February 2027; Morocco’s winter rainfall depends more on North Atlantic conditions, the agency told Hespress on Nov. 25.

ma.headline: Morocco mobilises nearly 22 billion dirhams for defence industry
ma.dek: Two agreements bring public funders, banks and market bodies into a plan targeting 50 billion dirhams in annual revenue, mostly from exports.
paragraphs: Morocco has mobilised nearly 22 billion dirhams from public partners to develop its defence and security industry, officials said at a signing ceremony in Rabat on Wednesday, 25 November. King Mohammed VI presided over the event, where two framework agreements were signed.

Ali Seddiki, director general of the Moroccan Agency for Investment and Export Development (AMDIE), announced the funding. One agreement finances the "Morocco Offer" roadmap; the other brings in domestic private and financial institutions. The programme aims eventually to generate at least 50 billion dirhams in annual revenue, with more than 65% from exports.

The second agreement includes Bank Al-Maghrib, the Moroccan banks' association, the Casablanca Stock Exchange and other financial bodies. A future strategic agency, named DIFAA (Defence Industry Strategic Agency), was also announced; the distribution of public funding among projects and the terms of private financing remain to be set.

ma.headline: Crédit du Maroc reports 19,1 % rise in consolidated net profit
ma.dek: The Moroccan bank’s consolidated banking net income increased 8,3 % to 2 900 MDH in the nine months to September.
paragraphs: Crédit du Maroc reported a 19,1 % increase in consolidated net profit for the nine months ended 30 September 2026, the bank said after its supervisory board met on 26 November. Its outstanding loans rose 12 % over 12 months to 65 021 MDH at end-September.

Business lending increased 6,2 % to 52 972 MDH, with equipment loans up 30,5 %, leasing up 28,4 % and property-development loans up 12,8 %. Household lending grew 4 % to 22 889 MDH, including an 11,4 % increase in consumer loans and a 2,2 % rise in housing loans.

Consolidated banking net income rose 8,3 % to 2 900 MDH, as interest margin and commissions offset weaker market operations. Net interest margin increased 11,4 % to 2 220 MDH, while commission income rose 3,5 % to 392 MDH.

ma.headline: Morocco tightens surveillance for 124,971 teacher exam candidates
ma.dek: The Education Ministry ordered online monitoring and automated cheating detection, with no more than 20 candidates in each room.
paragraphs: Morocco’s Education Ministry has ordered tighter monitoring for the November 28 written exams for entry to the country’s Regional Centers for Education and Training Professions. Nearly 125,000 candidates are due to sit the tests, with automated cheating detection and online monitoring among the measures.

An urgent directive to regional education authorities sets a limit of 20 candidates per room and requires at least two supervisors in each. Exam centers must keep reserve supervisors equal to 20% of their exam personnel, ban phones and other electronic devices, and appoint committees to address cheating attempts.

Central and regional monitoring units will track websites and social media groups carrying exam materials, suspected leaks or information about questions, according to the directive obtained by Hespress. Centers must report suspicious activity immediately to the central monitoring coordinator. Of 301,373 applications, 124,971 candidates were shortlisted, about 41.5%.

ma.headline: Morocco and Japan mark 70 years of diplomatic relations
ma.dek: At a Tokyo reception, Princess Takamado recalled exchanges between the Moroccan royal family and Japan’s imperial family and urged closer cooperation.
paragraphs: Princess Takamado of Japan highlighted the close historical ties between Morocco’s royal family and Japan’s imperial family at a reception in Tokyo on Thursday, as the countries marked 70 years of diplomatic relations. Morocco’s embassy in Japan organised the event.

In her speech, Takamado recalled visits and meetings that have shaped exchanges between the two families. She said their relationship reflected friendship and mutual esteem, and expressed hope that their ties of friendship and cooperation would grow stronger in the years ahead.
The reception focused on relations between the royal and imperial families, alongside the diplomatic anniversary.

ug.headline: Uganda charges six over alleged USh13 billion road compensation fraud
ug.dek: Prosecutors say inflated claims for structures on the planned Kasanje-Mpigi Expressway could have cost the government more than USh13 billion.
paragraphs: Six people have been charged in Mpigi over an alleged bid to take more than USh13 billion from the government through inflated compensation claims for properties on the planned Kasanje-Mpigi Expressway. They face charges of building without permission in a planning area.

Prosecutors allege that between February 2022 and December 2025 the accused and others still at large put up structures in Mmembe Makuku and Lufuka villages, on land already designated for the road, without development permits. The State House Anti-Corruption Unit says the accused also worked with officials from the Ministry of Works and Transport, among them former roads authority staff, surveyors and valuers, to inflate the value of the structures. The six were remanded until December 1.

The anti-corruption unit says it is still working to identify and arrest the officials and others it suspects of taking part. The arrests followed a visit by Works and Transport Minister Fred Byamukama, who asked the unit to look into compensation rates that he considered exorbitant.

ug.headline: Rwenzori farmers earn carbon income by planting trees
ug.dek: A Kasese farmer has received USh880,000 since 2021, while agroforestry is also supporting crops and livestock on his land.
paragraphs: Farmers on the slopes of Uganda’s Rwenzori Mountains are earning carbon-credit payments by planting and maintaining trees. William Ndeleghana, a farmer in Karambi village, Kasese district, has received USh880,000 since joining a tree-growing project in 2021, for trees on his 4.3 acres.

Ndeleghana says the payments have helped him pay school fees and improve his household income. Philimon Baluku Saalongo, another participant, received three payments of USh370,000 after tree assessments. He now grows coffee, bananas and cassava and keeps goats, chickens and pigs; he says trees have reduced erosion and water runoff on his land.

The Rwenzori Slopes Tree Farmers Cooperative Society has more than 2,500 members across five sub-counties and supports agroforestry, beekeeping, livestock projects and access to seedlings. It also runs a mobile money service.

ug.headline: Tayebwa urges Rotary to expand cancer and climate work in Uganda
ug.dek: The deputy speaker said Parliament contributed USh3 billion to the Rotary Cancer Run this year and called for larger environmental programmes.
paragraphs: Uganda’s Deputy Speaker Thomas Tayebwa urged Rotary International to expand its work on cancer and climate change during a meeting at Parliament in Kampala on Thursday. He said Parliament had contributed USh3 billion to the annual Rotary Cancer Run this year, part of more than USh10 billion given over the years.

Tayebwa said the cancer burden was growing in Uganda and other African countries, and that the initiative could grow. He also urged Rotary to scale up reforestation, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, freshwater conservation and waste management, and to mobilise young people on environmental conservation.

Rotary International President Olayinka Babalola thanked the government and Parliament for their role in immunisation and Uganda's elimination of indigenous wild poliovirus. Rotary directors and delegations are in Uganda for the 7th All-Africa Rotary Institute at Speke Resort Munyonyo.

paragraphs: President Yoweri Museveni directed Uganda’s prime minister to identify a Lake Victoria island for a proposed resort during a meeting with UK-based International Tourism Investment Corporation Limited at his Kisozi Farm on Friday, November 27. The company’s delegation, led by chief executive Ibrahim Ayoub, expressed interest in resorts, hotels and other tourism infrastructure.

Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja said Ayoub had returned to Uganda to advance investment discussions and formalise arrangements with government ministries. She said he was in talks with three international hotel groups about building hotels in the country. Museveni said the proposed resort would require about 100 acres and that the government could identify suitable land.

Museveni asked the company to consider less-developed islands in the Ssese group, which comprises about 82 islands, as well as islands in Buvuma and Mukono. He also suggested tourism facilities along the River Nile and near national parks.

ug.headline: Uganda pairs 2027 tourism expo with AFCON visitor push
ug.dek: The May event will bring together two regional expos weeks before Uganda co-hosts the football tournament with Kenya and Tanzania.
paragraphs: Uganda’s tourism board launched the 2027 Pearl of Africa Tourism Expo, to be held jointly with the East African Community Regional Tourism Expo in Kampala. The two events are scheduled for May 6-8 at Speke Resort Convention Centre, weeks before Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania co-host the Africa Cup of Nations from June 19 to July 17.

Tourism Board chief executive Juliana Kagwa said the campaign is designed to turn football visitors into longer-staying guests. At the previous expo, held over three days in May, 124 hosted buyers generated 7,745 business meetings and commitments worth about USh1.8 billion. The board remains in contact with 60% of those buyers, below its 75% target, Kagwa said.

Uganda Wildlife Authority executive director James Musinguzi called for more accommodation and domestic flights to destinations including Kidepo and Kisoro, and said some roads remain in poor condition. He said the authority would diversify wildlife-related products for the tourism board to market.

zw.headline: Zimbabwe approves state-funded bank for veterans’ businesses
zw.dek: The licensed microfinance bank will offer loans for farming, orders and emergencies before expanding into a deposit-taking institution over three to four years.
paragraphs: Zimbabwe’s Cabinet has approved a government-funded microfinance bank to lend to veterans of the liberation struggle, Information Minister Zhemu Soda said. The Veterans Microfinance Bank is intended to provide affordable credit for businesses using land, mining claims and farms allocated to ex-fighters.

Soda said a lack of affordable finance had limited veterans’ ability to use those assets. The bank will offer agribusiness and order-financing loans, personal and group lending, and emergency loans, alongside financial-literacy programmes and digital services. Women and young veterans are among its primary beneficiaries.

The bank will begin as a licensed microfinance institution under the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, then develop over three to four years into a deposit-taking, digitally enabled bank. It will be wholly owned by Veterans Investments Holding Company, with technical backing from the People’s Own Savings Bank.

zw.headline: Harare residents urge council to map flood risks and clear drains
zw.dek: The Combined Harare Residents Association says high-density and low-lying areas face the worst flooding as the rainy season intensifies.
paragraphs: The Combined Harare Residents Association (CHRA), a residents’ group, has urged Harare City Council to map flood-prone areas and clear blocked drains as flooding worsens across the city during the rainy season. In a statement issued on Thursday, 26 November, it said high-density suburbs and low-lying areas were worst affected.

CHRA said flooded homes, damaged roads and disrupted movement recur each rainy season, while water contamination raises public-health risks. Flooded roads and public spaces in the city centre have also disrupted businesses and travel, the association said. It called for drains and channels to be cleared and repaired, roads to be maintained, and areas most at risk to be mapped so the council can direct limited resources to exposed communities.

The association also urged the council to prevent developments that block natural waterways and build new infrastructure where existing systems cannot cope. It said mapping should guide rehabilitation and investment priorities.

zw.headline: Zimbabwe needs US$52.78 million to clear remaining landmines by 2030
zw.dek: Deputy Defence Minister Levy Mayihlome says more than 97% of contaminated land has been cleared, with about 22,000 households set to benefit.
paragraphs: Zimbabwe needs US$52.78 million to clear its remaining landmines by December 2030, Deputy Minister of Defence Levy Mayihlome said during a field visit to Rushinga District in Mashonaland Central on Wednesday. He said more than 97% of the country's mine-contaminated land had already been cleared by the Government working with international partners.

Under Project RECLAIM, a US$3.35 million initiative backed by Japan and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), demining in Rushinga and Mudzi has released 221,016 square metres and destroyed 2,746 anti-personnel mines. Japan has committed about US$2.95 million and the UNDP US$400,000. Japan's ambassador, Maekawa Nobutaka, said the work would directly benefit about 22,000 households.

Zimbabwe inherited an estimated three million landmines across eight major minefields stretching about 850km along its borders after independence in 1980. Mayihlome said the Government will keep financing the National Mine Clearance Unit until the task is complete.

zw.headline: Manica Diamonds dissolved, leaving Mutare without a top-flight club in 2027
zw.dek: The Gem Boys end nine years in Zimbabwean football, a run that took them from Eastern Region Division One to the Castle Lager Premier Soccer League.
paragraphs: Manica Diamonds has been dissolved after nine years in Zimbabwean football, leaving the city of Mutare without a Premier Soccer League representative in 2027. The club, known as the Gem Boys, had climbed from the Eastern Region Division One to the top flight.
The dissolution ends a journey that brought top-flight football back to Mutare. NewsDay Zimbabwe reported the closure but gave no financial details or reason for the decision.
Recent developments at Sakubva Stadium did not change the outcome for the city, which will have no Premier Soccer League club next season.

zw.headline: Zimbabwe ministers tour Kenya's Konza smart city for Mt Hampden plan
zw.dek: Three ministers, the Central Intelligence Organisation director-general and a waste-management adviser to President Emmerson Mnangagwa made the visit.
paragraphs: A delegation of Zimbabwean government officials toured Kenya's Konza Technopolis on Friday to study its smart-city system. The visit was aimed at how the system could shape Zimbabwe's proposed smart city in Mt Hampden.

The delegation comprised Justice Minister Ziyambi Ziyambi, National Housing and Social Amenities Minister Paul Mavima, Transport Minister Felix Mhona and Central Intelligence Organisation director-general Paul Chikawa. They were joined by Dilesh Nguwaya, executive chairman of Geo Pomona Waste Management, who is also a special adviser to President Emmerson Mnangagwa on waste management and environmental sustainability.
The report gives no decision, agreement or timetable for the Mt Hampden project.

cv.headline: Cape Verde plans new water and sewer connections in Praia for 2027
cv.dek: The 2027 state budget proposal allocates about 1,3 billion escudos to water and sanitation as the minister cites losses above 60% in the public network.
paragraphs: Cape Verde’s Environment, Climate Action and Energy Minister Carlos Varela said Praia is expected to gain around 1,000 water and sewer network connections in 2027. He announced the plan during debate on the 2027 state budget proposal in the National Assembly.

Varela said losses in the public network exceed 60%, a burden he described as unsustainable for water-supply companies. He also said the country lacks enough water storage to keep supplies going if production stops, and cited continuing supply problems on Maio and Boa Vista.

The budget proposal sets aside about 1,3 billion escudos for water and sanitation within a package of approximately 5,2 billion escudos for energy, water, sanitation, environment, biodiversity and climate action.

cv.headline: Cape Verde suspends hotel kitchen, buffet and storeroom on Sal
cv.dek: Inspectors cited pests, rat droppings and unsafe food storage; the hotel also failed to return the tourist tax from July 2026.
paragraphs: Cape Verde’s economic activities inspectorate ordered a hotel on Sal to suspend work immediately in its kitchen, buffet and storeroom after inspectors found hygiene and food-safety violations. The hotel’s name was not disclosed.

The inspection team included the inspectorate, health officials, national and municipal police, and tourism technicians. It reported pests, rat droppings, poor cleaning and food stored incorrectly. The authorities said they acted to prevent customers from eating potentially contaminated food.
Inspectors also found that the hotel had not returned the tourist tax since July 2026. A formal administrative offence case will be opened, and the hotel faces a fine of two million escudos.

cv.headline: Cape Verde security essay calls for lasting prevention and police coordination
cv.dek: Domingos Barbosa da Silva says short-lived community policing and weak information-sharing leave the causes of crime unaddressed.
paragraphs: Domingos Barbosa da Silva argues that Cape Verde’s security policy relies too heavily on police operations and tough-on-crime rhetoric, while prevention and social reintegration receive too little attention. He points to youth crime, urban violence, domestic violence, drug trafficking and insecurity in neighbourhoods as challenges facing the country.

Silva says pilot community-policing projects lose effect through staff rotation, scarce dedicated resources and a lack of continuity. He also argues that the National Police, Judicial Police, municipal police, Armed Forces and Public Prosecutor’s Office need to share information to anticipate crime; institutional barriers and duplicated work weaken that capacity.

His proposed prevention framework spans social conditions, people or places at risk, and efforts to prevent reoffending. Silva says responses should address school dropout, opportunities for young people, leisure activities and inclusive neighbourhood planning, alongside effective reintegration programmes for former prisoners.

cv.headline: Praia hosts six-day Brazil-Cape Verde cinema event
cv.dek: The programme pairs Cape Verdean environmental films with Brazilian street cinema and conversations encouraging students to make short videos.
paragraphs: Praia is hosting a six-day Brazil-Cape Verde cinema event featuring films from both countries, Cândida Barros, president of the Cape Verdean association ACACV, told Expresso das Ilhas. The event is intended to promote the countries’ films and bring their cultures together.

Cape Verde will show environmental films, while Brazilian filmmaker Eudaldo Monção Jr. will present street cinema from Brazil and films he produces there. Barros said global warming will be a central theme, with conversations aimed at encouraging students to make short videos and write about environmental preservation.

The programme also includes film-related training and visits to the Tabanca Museum and the Traditional Pottery Interpretive Centre, both in Assomada, as well as a visit to Cinema da Praia. The event is a partnership involving ACACV, the Guimarães Rosa Institute, Salvador-based Memorabilia Filmes and the Ribeira Grande de Santiago municipal council.

td.headline: Chad aid reaches 2.5 million people as funding covers 46.3% of needs
td.dek: The response had reached 75% of its initial target by 30 September, but nearly one million people in need remained without assistance.
paragraphs: Humanitarian agencies in Chad had provided aid in at least one sector to about 2.5 million people by 30 September 2026, despite a shortfall in funding for the 2026 response plan. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported that about 4.5 million people needed assistance in the country.

The plan had targeted 3.4 million people, but budget restrictions led aid groups to narrow their focus to 1.9 million people with the most critical needs. Of those reached, 1.4 million had priority needs, equal to 74% of the reprioritised group.

Partners had raised $456.3 million, or 46.3% of the plan’s total funding requirement. Coverage was lowest for coordination and camp management at 6.9%, refugee response at 10.1% and nutrition at 29.3%. More resources are needed to reach half a million people in areas of high humanitarian tension.

td.headline: Chad’s Déby takes CEEAC chair, pledges focus on implementation
td.dek: The Central African bloc’s new leader set out priorities including peace, security, economic integration and infrastructure development.
paragraphs: Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno became rotating chair of the Economic Community of Central African States (CEEAC) at its 27th ordinary summit on 27 November in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea. He outlined priorities for his term that include peace, security, economic integration and infrastructure development.

Déby said the bloc’s main challenge was putting its policies and decisions into effect. Central Africa has natural, energy, agricultural, forest and water resources, but faces conflicts, insecurity, economic and financial difficulties, weak trade among member states, inadequate infrastructure and barriers to movement of people and goods.

He said the presidency should turn the region’s potential into tangible results for its citizens. Déby also thanked member-state leaders for choosing him and praised outgoing chair Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who led the bloc for three years.

td.headline: Chad pilgrimage regulator chief denies alleged UAE account transfers
td.dek: A judicial document cites transfers of 20 million and 16.5 million dirhams from the regulator’s accounts to a personal account at First Abu Dhabi Bank.
paragraphs: Idriss Dokony Adiker, president of Chad’s pilgrimage regulator, denied on Friday that he made, ordered or benefited from two alleged transfers to a personal account in the United Arab Emirates. A judicial document dated 23 October cites transfers of 20 million and 16.5 million dirhams from the regulator’s accounts.

In a statement released on 27 November, Adiker said the allegations appeared in a prosecutor’s request issued to carry out an order by the Supreme Court president. He said the regulator’s Saudi account is used for electronic payment of Hajj services under Saudi authorities’ control, and that the institution’s 2025 financial balances are documented in its accounts and audit report.

Adiker said he had received no official notice or request for an explanation from the government or his superiors. He said he was prepared to provide supporting documents to judicial authorities and reserved the right to take legal action.

dj.headline: Regional body adopts Djibouti’s anti-money-laundering report
dj.dek: The evaluation recognised reforms and stronger coordination, while examining how the country’s rules work in practice.
paragraphs: A regional body adopted Djibouti’s anti-money-laundering evaluation report at a session that opened on 21 November in the United Arab Emirates’ capital. The adoption was Djibouti’s main result from the meeting, the Djiboutian News Agency reported.

Member countries praised reforms to Djibouti’s legal, institutional and operational framework, including better coordination among government agencies. Interior Minister Omar Abdi Said led the delegation, which included the central bank governor and the head of the national technical committee. The evaluation considers both the rules and how they are applied, the report said.

Djibouti’s national coordinator, Djama Souleiman, said the country intended to continue strengthening its system. Countries judged insufficient in such reviews can face enhanced monitoring, known as the “grey list,” which can weigh on foreign bank relations and the ability to attract investors.

dj.headline: Djibouti customs and partners turn to electronic single-window report
dj.dek: The planned system is meant to support trade facilitation and regional integration, with South Korea's Cupia responsible for much of the technical work.
paragraphs: Djibouti's customs administration and its partners are due to work on a consultation report for the country's planned electronic single window, the national customs authority said. The partners include the Ministry of Trade, the secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area and Cupia, a South Korean agency.

The report followed months of work by customs officials and partners on the opportunities the system could open, including Djibouti's role in regional integration. Cupia, which the authority said carries much of the project's technical delivery, has previously worked on similar systems in Ethiopia, Tanzania and Ghana.
The project is tied to the African Continental Free Trade Area's push to deepen economic integration and make trade within Africa easier.

dj.headline: Adenka opens Djibouti office to serve businesses and investors
dj.dek: The Abidjan-based audit network says its Djibouti team will offer accounting, tax and risk advice alongside audits and project assurance.
paragraphs: Adenka, an independent African audit and accounting network, has opened an office in Djibouti, extending its operations into East Africa. Founder Marc Wabi launched the network in Abidjan in May 2025; its headquarters remain there. The Djibouti office is led by Bilane Houssein Djama, a chartered accountant and managing partner.

Adenka offers audits and assurance, including statutory accounts and project audits, as well as accounting and advisory services covering tax, risk management, strategy, digital transformation and cybersecurity. Wabi said the network targets private companies, especially small and family-owned businesses, as well as public institutions and foreign investors seeking greater transparency and confidence.

Adenka says it already operates in Côte d’Ivoire, Benin, Senegal, Congo, Gabon and Guinea, and can cover about 20 African markets. Wabi, who spent 27 years at Deloitte, said the network chose Djibouti for its ports, logistics corridors and free zones.

dj.headline: Djibouti urges UN rules on autonomous weapons and drone threats
dj.dek: Ambassador Mohamed Siad Doualeh called for human control over force and stronger safeguards for shipping, ports and undersea cables.
paragraphs: Djibouti’s ambassador to the United Nations called for legally binding rules to prohibit and regulate autonomous weapons, saying decisions to kill must remain under effective human control. Mohamed Siad Doualeh spoke at a high-level public debate on conflict amid rapid technological change.

Doualeh also urged an international regulatory framework for unmanned drones and stronger cooperation to protect seafarers, commercial ships, ports and undersea cables. He said small states and developing countries needed help confronting these threats.

The ambassador cited attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea since late 2023, claimed by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, and damage to several undersea cables. He said those incidents exposed the vulnerability of infrastructure supporting global trade and communications.

The race started at 16h00 at Place Menelik. Air Djibouti and the Djiboutian Athletics Federation organised the competition, which also included a 2 km race for men with special needs, won by Abdoulrazack Bouh Roble in 6 min 02 sec.

sz.headline: Eswatini Cabinet endorses corruption inquiry
sz.dek: The government says the judicial investigation follows a parliamentary motion, as reported monthly losses from corruption rise to E90 million.
paragraphs: Eswatini’s Cabinet has endorsed a judicial inquiry into corruption, following a motion passed recently in Parliament, Agriculture Minister Mandla Tshawuka said at a media engagement in Mbabane. The endorsement advances a call for an investigation, but no start date was given.

Finance Minister Neal Rijkenberg said estimated losses to corruption had increased to E90 million a month, from E80 million in earlier years. He acknowledged that the Anti-Corruption Commission had secured no convictions in recent years and said ministers responsible for foreign affairs and justice had worked to resolve institutional issues affecting the commission.
Rijkenberg said he hoped changes to the institutional arrangements would help the relevant bodies carry out their responsibilities more effectively.

sz.headline: Eswatini’s family-planning association traces its 50-year rise
sz.dek: Family Life Association of Eswatini grew from efforts to address unplanned pregnancies into a provider of services and education across the country.
paragraphs: Family Life Association of Eswatini (FLAS), also known as Temndeni, will mark its 50th birthday next year, the organisation’s renewal celebration heard. Fiona Duby, who helped establish it after arriving in Swaziland in 1976, recounted its beginnings in response to unplanned pregnancies and young people’s need for non-judgmental information.

Duby said Manzini town treasurer David Sibandze and King Sobhuza clinic head nurse Eunice Sowazi helped develop the idea. St Theresa’s High School, where Duby taught, was losing about 50 girls a year to unplanned pregnancy; the school asked her to teach sex education and let her work at the clinic one day a week. She spent at least two years consulting government ministries, churches, universities and the Royal Family, and secured long-term support from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), Washington’s foreign aid agency.

FLAS later expanded life-planning education to schools nationwide and family-planning services to Manzini, Malkerns and Mbabane. Duby left Swaziland in 1984, when Cabinet was set to transfer the country’s membership of the International Planned Parenthood Federation to FLAS.

She graduated from Northwestern University in 2023 with a bachelor’s degree in civil and environmental engineering.

Mngometulu said her work includes technical reports, cost estimates and designs, as well as construction-site visits and meetings with officials. ga.headline: Oligui Nguema joins CEEAC summit talks on regional integration
ga.dek: The Gabonese president is taking part in discussions in Malabo on security, trade across borders and cooperation in energy and health.
paragraphs: Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema left Libreville on 26 November for the 27th ordinary session of the Economic Community of Central African States (CEEAC) leaders’ conference in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea. The meeting is scheduled for Friday 27 November, with security, economic integration and cooperation among the listed subjects.

The leaders are due to discuss security crises, maritime security and border governance, as well as the CEEAC Vision 2050 and its 2026-2030 indicative strategic plan. Energy and health cooperation are also on the agenda, according to Gabon Review.

The trip follows a 10 November meeting in Libreville between Oligui Nguema and an envoy of Equatorial Guinea’s president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo. Their talks included aligning the two countries’ positions in CEEAC and the Central African Economic and Monetary Community.

ga.headline: Gabon opens cybersecurity forum with push for local data hosting
ga.dek: The Libreville event brought together about 400 participants to discuss digital sovereignty, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.
paragraphs: Gabon’s third Cybersecurity Forum opened on 27 November at the Aninf Tower in Libreville, with organisers calling for stronger national cybersecurity capacity and local data hosting. The event was organised by the National Agency for Digital Infrastructure and Frequencies (Aninf), ST Digital and CNConsulting.

About 400 people attended, including public decision-makers, business leaders, technology and security specialists, and diplomatic representatives. Aninf director-general Alberto Wenceslas Mounguengui Moudoki called for public and private sector cooperation. The forum’s stated goals also include encouraging technology partnerships.

ST Digital director-general Laïka Mba said the event had become a gathering for Gabonese working in technology and cybersecurity. Ambassador Noël Nelson Messone, a former minister of new technologies, delivered the opening lecture on the diplomatic stakes of cybersecurity in Africa.

ga.headline: Gabon police extend Libreville night patrols through December
ga.dek: Teams searched streets and checked residents in five neighborhoods after reports of assaults and night burglaries in the capital.
paragraphs: Gabon’s National Police sent teams through five Libreville neighborhoods on the night of 25-26 November, launching patrols that are scheduled to continue throughout December. Officers went to Baie des Cochons, Akébé, Petit-Paris, Carrefour-Hassan and Cocotiers.

The police used foot patrols and vehicles to check people and enter alleyways, Gabon Review reported. Residents welcomed the presence, with several describing robberies and threats involving bladed weapons in their neighborhoods. The police said the operation aims to prevent assaults, burglaries and other offences.

During the patrol, officers found the body of a man in his forties in Akébé after he was struck by a vehicle whose driver fled. On 25 November, Interior Minister Edgard Moukoumbi also met senior police officials to discuss how to apply the government’s security roadmap.

ga.headline: Gabon’s vice-president courts Rwandan agriculture investor
ga.dek: KT Hub Ltd. wants to expand into Gabon and has begun steps to set up locally after meeting Alexandre Barro Chambrier in Kigali.
paragraphs: Gabon Vice-President Alexandre Barro Chambrier met KT Hub Ltd., a Rwandan agricultural company, in Kigali to discuss investment and support for Gabon’s food production. Chambrier was in the Rwandan capital for the YouthConnekt Africa summit, where he represented President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema.

KT Hub’s delegation was led by chief executive Theoneste Kabahizi. The company said it wants to bring its agricultural experience to Gabon and has approached the Agriculture Ministry and the National Agency for Investment Promotion. It has also started setting up a local structure, while asking for help to speed its establishment.
The company’s representatives plan to return to Gabon in January to continue discussions. The government has said it wants to reduce the country’s reliance on food imports.

gm.headline: Gambians vote December 5 as Barrow seeks a third term
gm.dek: The election pits the president against opposition leader Ousainou Darboe and six other candidates, with presidential term limits still absent from the constitution.
paragraphs: Gambians vote on December 5 in a presidential election that will decide whether Adama Barrow wins a third term. Barrow, who took office in 2017 after Yahya Jammeh’s 22-year rule ended, is running despite an earlier pledge not to seek another term.

His challengers include Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda and four other candidates. The ballot comes under the 1997 constitution, adopted during Jammeh’s rule; a proposed replacement with presidential term limits failed to win the required three-quarter majority in the National Assembly in July 2025.

Barrow says voters should decide who leads Gambia and supports term limits, but says they depend on parliamentary backing for a new constitution. During campaign stops in Kiang, he cited roads, electricity and water services as reasons to re-elect him.

gm.headline: Bensouda challenges reported D4.9 billion vehicle spending
gm.dek: The presidential candidate said rural communities need better services and pledged to redirect public resources and improve farmers’ access to finance.
paragraphs: Talib Ahmed Bensouda, a presidential candidate, questioned reported government spending of D4.9 billion on vehicles during a campaign tour of the Lower River Region. He argued the money should have gone toward development needs in rural communities.

Bensouda cited shortages of water, poor healthcare facilities, limited education and unemployment. He said he would cut excessive spending on salaries, allowances and per diems and redirect public resources to improve livelihoods. At Jarambeleh, he proposed an agricultural bank to help farmers obtain financing and support.

At Soma, regional chairman Alagie Sillah raised electricity and water shortages, while women farmers called for more support and crop-processing machines. Bensouda also linked unemployment, poverty and poor governance to young Gambians’ dangerous journeys abroad.

paragraphs: Prince Ebrahim Sanyang, leader of the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), pledged to launch Gambia International Airways and establish a D8 million milling company in Kiang if opposition candidate Ousainou Darboe wins the December 5 presidential election. Sanyang said the airline would open within 30 days of a Darboe victory. He said milling machines were stored in a Banjul warehouse and ready to be handed to the Kiang Association to manage. He also pledged D100,000 for a youth sports development fund, to be given to Landing B. Sanneh, chairman of Mansa Konko Area Council, to oversee.
Sanyang is part of the UDP-led Gambia First Alliance. He told supporters that investors had lost confidence in the Barrow administration and were seeking change; that was his assessment.

gm.headline: Unite Coalition pledges regional mini stadiums and Senegambia League
gm.dek: Presidential candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda made the sports pledges at a campaign rally in Jabang, where residents appealed for a proper playing ground.
paragraphs: The opposition Unite Coalition has pledged a mini stadium in every region and a Senegambia League for first-division clubs if it wins The Gambia’s December presidential election. Presidential candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda announced the plans at a campaign rally in Jabang, in the Old Yundum constituency, during the coalition’s first stop in the Kombo area.

Bensouda said every constituency would also get facilities for basketball, volleyball and other sports. Sheik Hatab Hydara, coordinator of the Unite Movement in Jabang Ward, asked coalition leaders to complete the community’s sandy football pitch, which residents say is unsuitable for regular play.

The coalition says it would encourage private-sector partnerships with divisional teams to raise companies’ visibility and give clubs new income. Bensouda described the proposed league as an extension of the existing divisional system.

gm.headline: Gambian journalist Mustapha K. Darboe wins Abuja investigative journalism award
gm.dek: Darboe was recognised for a report on a multi-million-dollar Gambian government venture that made the President's nephew a major food importer.
paragraphs: Mustapha K. Darboe, Editor-in-Chief of the investigative outlet The Republic, won the Social Accountability (Investigative Journalism) category at the annual Excellence in Journalism Awards in Abuja, Nigeria. He received the award on Wednesday at a ceremony organised by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

He was honoured for his report "Inside the multi-million-dollar Gambia gov't venture that makes president's nephew a major food importer", which examined a government venture and its links to the President's nephew. The award recognises his work on transparency, accountability and public interest reporting.
The Point congratulated Darboe on the win, describing it as putting Gambian journalism on the international stage.

gn.headline: IMF approves $425 million programme for Guinea, leaves subsidy cuts to government
gn.dek: The 2026-2029 deal calls for a strategy to reduce subsidies, while Guinea decides when to act and strengthens support for vulnerable households.
paragraphs: The International Monetary Fund’s board approved a 2026-2029 economic programme for Guinea on 23 November, providing 310.59 million special drawing rights, or about $425 million. On Friday, the IMF’s resident representative in Guinea, Dr Nérée Noumon, said the agreement did not require the government to cut subsidies immediately.

Noumon said Guinea would first need consultations, public communication and measures to support affected people before deciding when to pursue a subsidy-reduction strategy. The programme commits the authorities to strengthening social targeting; the IMF said more than 80% of subsidies currently benefit the wealthiest 20% of households. Noumon cited the Nafa programme and the unified social registry, which he said was not yet fully operational.

The IMF plans to provide technical assistance and help build the authorities’ capacity during the reforms, Noumon said. He said transport and other services would also need to be considered when identifying vulnerable people.

gn.headline: Guinea plans new fuel depot and reforms power utility
gn.dek: Economy Minister Mariama Ciré Sylla says studies for the depot are complete as the government works to improve the utility’s governance.
paragraphs: Guinea has completed studies for a new fuel depot and put a reform plan in place for state power utility EDG, Economy Minister Mariama Ciré Sylla said at a news conference on the 2026-2029 economic programme with the International Monetary Fund. The country has faced daytime electricity cuts in Conakry and difficulties securing fuel since an explosion at its hydrocarbons depot two years ago.

Sylla said the EDG plan is intended to improve governance and efficiency, while construction of the depot would give the country more flexibility in fuel supply. She said the government wants to move quickly on the project. The government has kept the pump price of fuel at 12 000 GNF, she said.

Sylla said fuel prices in 2027 would be assessed in light of changes in international oil prices. She also said the IMF programme would help the government rationalise subsidies and direct support towards vulnerable people, while protecting household purchasing power.

gn.headline: Mauritania intercepts 94 young Guineans bound for the Canary Islands
gn.dek: Mauritanian coast guards stopped the boat off Nouadhibou on 19 November, and the group is now being housed in Rosso while it waits for travel documents.
paragraphs: Mauritanian coast guards intercepted 94 young Guineans off Nouadhibou on 19 November, aboard a boat heading for the Canary Islands. The group had left the artisanal port of Boffa, in Lower Guinea, on 13 November.

Mauritanian authorities said the boat was in distress when they intervened. The migrants were taken to Rosso, on the Mauritania-Senegal border, where several are reported to have serious health problems and to describe precarious living conditions.

Mohamed Keita, the local representative of the Council of Guineans in Mauritania, is hosting and caring for them while they wait for travel permits. The group is asking for help to return to Guinea. No deaths have been reported among those counted, though many cases of illness have been noted.

gn.headline: Guinea suspends Infosbruts and director for three months
gn.dek: The media regulator said the site published electoral propaganda for a Lélouma Senate candidate before the Supreme Court issued its final candidate list.
paragraphs: Guinea’s High Authority for Communication (HAC), the media regulator, suspended the Infosbruts news site and its publishing director, journalist Idrissa Sampiring Diallo, for three months on Friday, 27 November. The order took effect on the date it was signed.

The HAC said Infosbruts had carried content it considered electoral propaganda in favour of a Senate candidate in Lélouma prefecture. Its decision said the publication violated election rules because it appeared before the Supreme Court published the final list of candidates.

During the suspension, the site is barred from publishing and Diallo from journalistic activity anywhere in Guinea, the regulator said. In a letter reported by Guinee Matin, Diallo apologised for a publication he said was made inadvertently and accepted responsibility.

gw.headline: Guinea-Bissau delays presidential and parliamentary elections until 2028
gw.dek: Gen Horta N'Tam's decree moves the polls from 6 December to 26 November 2028, extending the military-led transition beyond its promised 12 months.
paragraphs: Guinea-Bissau's transitional president, Gen Horta N'Tam, has postponed presidential and parliamentary elections from 6 December to 26 November 2028, delaying the planned return to civilian rule by two years.

The presidency said an assessment found insufficient technical, material and financial conditions to hold the polls as scheduled. It said the delay would allow more time for credible, transparent and inclusive elections, with equal opportunities for candidates.

The military seized power in November 2025 and had promised to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months. The presidency reaffirmed plans for the country's first local government elections but gave no date.

gw.headline: Simão Mendes hospital workers press for 11 months of overdue allowances
gw.dek: The hospital administrator says the government committed to pay three months, while staff also seek eight months of pay for contract workers.
paragraphs: Workers at Guinea-Bissau’s Simão Mendes National Hospital held a vigil outside the facility on Friday, 27 November, demanding 11 months of unpaid allowances and overtime. They also seek eight months of remuneration for staff hired on service contracts, better working conditions and more medical equipment.

Óscar Bassangue, the hospital workers’ union representative, cited delayed pay, shortages of supplies and poor conditions in several departments, including the oxygen production centre. Hospital administrator Braia Naquidum said services continued during the protest and the workers’ concerns had been discussed with the Finance Ministry and prime minister.

Naquidum said the government had committed to paying three months of overdue allowances. He said the oxygen plant was operating below capacity because it needed maintenance, and that the company responsible had been contacted to restore normal operations. Bassangue said the vigils would continue weekly until the demands were met.

lr.headline: Liberia’s Senate orders inquiry into banknote shortage and high prices
lr.dek: The committee is due to examine delays in releasing up to L$79 billion in authorized notes and why currency gains have not lowered commodity prices.
paragraphs: Liberia’s Senate ordered an investigation into the shortage of Liberian dollar banknotes and high prices of basic goods, directing its Committee on Banking and Currency to report to lawmakers on December 1. The decision followed concerns raised by River Gee County Senator Jonathan Sogbie on November 26.

Sogbie asked the Central Bank of Liberia governor and other officials to explain the shortage, progress printing up to L$79 billion in authorized notes, and delays in making them available. The Legislature authorized the printing between 2026 and 2030, mainly to replace worn and damaged notes. The Central Bank said the exchange rate was about L$163 to US$1.

The Senate committee is expected to engage the central bank and submit findings and recommendations to the full Senate. Sogbie also questioned why the Liberian dollar’s recent appreciation had not brought down prices of goods and services.

lr.headline: Liberia’s agriculture minister warns El Niño could cut rice yields by 30 to 50%
lr.dek: Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah told lawmakers that erratic rains and heat could disrupt planting and leave rice farmers with little or no harvest.
paragraphs: Liberia’s Agriculture Minister Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah and Environmental Protection Agency Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo warned the House of Representatives that a potential El Niño could disrupt planting and reduce food production. They said several counties were already experiencing severe dryness.

Nuetah said failed rains after March planting could destroy crops, while excessive rain could rot seeds before they germinate. Rice varieties take 90 days to 150 days to mature, and a shortened rainy season could leave longer-growing crops without enough water during flowering. Severe El Niño conditions could cut rice yields by 30 to 50% for crops planted during the affected period, he said.
The officials warned that flooding could also submerge swamp rice already planted. Nuetah said the risks extend to rural communities that depend heavily on rice production.

lr.headline: Liberia’s petroleum regulator sets 2027 deadline for first sector report
lr.dek: The five-year plan also follows US$13.8 million in budget contributions and eight production-sharing contracts ratified by lawmakers.
paragraphs: Liberia’s Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA) launched a five-year plan in Monrovia on Thursday, setting out priorities for the oil and gas industry through 2030 and promising its first State of the Petroleum Sector Report in 2027. Director General Marilyn T. Logan said the roadmap is intended to strengthen regulation, attract investment and build local technical expertise.

Logan said the authority contributed US$13.8 million to Liberia’s national budget over the past three years. She also said Liberia had gone more than a decade without a new Production Sharing Contract before the current leadership took office in March 2024; since then, the authority signed eight, all ratified by the Legislature.

The LPRA said reconnaissance is underway in the Harper Basin, and its 2026 Direct Negotiation Licensing Round, launched last month, is expected to beat its 2025 results. The plan includes contract management, environmental protection and transparency.

lr.headline: Liberia's House sends US$5.7 billion Bea Mountain deal for review
lr.dek: The proposed agreement includes 270 megawatts of power projects and road construction, but still needs legislative review and ratification.
paragraphs: Liberia's House of Representatives has referred a proposed US$5.7 billion infrastructure agreement with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation to two committees for review. The House acted Thursday after President Joseph Nyuma Boakai submitted the deal for legislative consideration and ratification.

The committees on Investment and Concessions and Public Works are expected to report to the full House within two weeks. The agreement would let Bea Mountain finance infrastructure, with approved spending offset against specified entitlements and corresponding government obligations.

Proposed works include three hydropower plants and a biomass plant, together rated at 270 megawatts, plus transmission lines and upgrades to the national electricity grid. The deal also lists roads in several counties and bridge and road work in Montserrado County; it remains subject to legislative approval.

lr.headline: Liberia coalition asks lawmakers to ratify workplace harassment convention
lr.dek: The nine-member coalition petitioned the House of Representatives, citing harassment and abuse affecting workers, especially women and vulnerable groups.
paragraphs: A coalition of nine trade unions, civil society organisations and government institutions petitioned Liberia’s House of Representatives on November 26 to ratify and implement the International Labour Organization’s Convention 190 on violence and harassment at work. The group asked lawmakers to take legislative steps toward adopting the convention.

The coalition said workers, particularly women, marginalised groups and people in vulnerable employment, face harassment, threats and exploitation. It cited 3,381 gender-based violence cases recorded in Liberia in 2024, with women and girls making up about 85% of survivors, while stressing that the figures were not limited to workplace incidents.

The group also cited 3,204 reported gender-based violence cases in 2023 and said workers fear dismissal, retaliation, stigma and discrimination when reporting abuse. Convention 190 was adopted in 2019.

ly.headline: Benghazi teachers end strike as 139 million dinars are allocated
ly.dek: The funds cover salary differences and session-based teaching allowances, with the first payments scheduled to start on November 30.
paragraphs: Teachers in Benghazi, Libya, have ended their strike and the new academic year has begun after the city's education supervisor received two checks totalling 139 million dinars for outstanding salary differences and teaching allowances.

Education supervisor Belaid Jumaa said 92 million dinars will cover salary differences, with each teacher due 2,000 dinars; distribution is scheduled to begin on Monday, November 30. A further 47 million dinars is for session-based teachers' allowances, with payments expected to reach their accounts in the coming days.

Jumaa said a unified salary schedule is postponed to allow parliamentary committees to review it before it goes to the House of Representatives. Graduates are due to be appointed to teaching shortages in several subjects from mid-December.

ly.headline: Ru’ya warns of up to 100 millimeters of rain in northwest Libya
ly.dek: The foundation says the heaviest downpours are expected around Tripoli and along the coast, with flash floods and road disruption possible.
paragraphs: The Ru’ya Foundation for Space Sciences and Its Applications warned Thursday evening that a cold front would bring thunderstorms and heavy rain to northwest Libya from Thursday night into early Friday. Rainfall is forecast at 20 to 60 millimeters, with local totals approaching 100 millimeters, especially in some coastal areas.

The foundation’s bulletin identifies greater Tripoli and the coast from Sabratha to Khoms among the areas expecting the heaviest rain. It also lists south of Tripoli, parts of the Jafara Plain and eastern parts of the Western Mountains, including Gharyan and Tarhuna. Most rain could fall within a few hours, the bulletin says.

The foundation warned of flash floods in valleys and mountain streams, water accumulation in low-lying and coastal areas, reduced visibility and possible road closures. It urged residents to avoid flood-prone areas and called on authorities and emergency services to raise their readiness.

mg.headline: Madagascar's ousted Assembly president asks court to annul his removal
mg.dek: Siteny Randrianasoloniaiko's petition also challenges the removal of three other bureau members, arguing the required serious grounds were not shown.
paragraphs: Siteny Randrianasoloniaiko, the former president of Madagascar's National Assembly, filed a petition with the High Constitutional Court on Friday, 27 November, seeking annulment of the Assembly's vote that removed him and three other members of its permanent bureau. Lawmakers had elected Marco Tsaradia, the only candidate, to succeed him on 25 November.

The petition contests the Assembly's resolution and asks the court to check whether the constitution's requirement of a serious reason against each member was met. The other three removed members are Christian Afakandro, Issa Charles Ibrahim and Charlot Mamihaja. The Assembly voted 112 to 37 to remove Randrianasoloniaiko, above the 109 votes its rules required.

His lawyers, from the Fanomezantsoa Heriniaina firm, argue that the court's October 2025 decision keeping existing institutions in place should also keep him in office. The handover ceremony with Tsaradia, which had been set for 27 November, remains in suspense while the court considers the case.

mg.headline: Madagascar plans more water for Antananarivo's outskirts
mg.dek: Three station upgrades are planned to add 10 800 m³ of drinking water a day to Jirama's network and serve districts around the capital.
paragraphs: Madagascar's water-access programme, known as PAAEP, plans to add 10 800 m³ of drinking water each day to Jirama's network by upgrading stations at Vontovorona, Ankadivoribe and Faralaza around Antananarivo. The work is intended to rehabilitate ageing facilities and protect household supply during the dry season.

At Vontovorona, a new treatment unit is planned to raise output to 300 m³ per hour, or 7 200 m³ per day. Engineer Andriatovohasina Tsifohimbola said a pump drawing from the Andromba River is expected to feed the existing lake, allowing use of an upper reservoir and improving supply from Fenoarivo to Ampitatafika Atsimo. The installation is scheduled to be operational by late 2027.

Ankadivoribe is set to draw from the Sisaony River and use an artificial pre-settling lake, with planned output of 250 m³ per hour for Soalandry, Ankadivoribe and Iavoloha. Faralaza's capacity is due to reach 400 m³ per hour through new boreholes and basins, serving Ambohidratrimo, Talatamaty and Ivato.

mg.headline: Ravatomanga family seeks answers over search of its tomb
mg.dek: Lawyers say people claiming a prosecutor’s mandate searched the family tomb in Moratsiazo and reported finding nothing.
paragraphs: Lawyers for the family of Mamy Ravatomanga, a Malagasy businessman imprisoned in Mauritius, are demanding explanations from Madagascar’s judicial authorities after his family tomb was searched in Moratsiazo, Soamahamanina, on Thursday 26 November 2026. The family’s statement says people who claimed to have been authorised by the public prosecutor carried out the operation.

The lawyers said the visitors reported finding nothing, and the family’s statement did not report any seizure. They are asking who took part, which judicial authority ordered the search and what legal acts authorised it. The nature of the search was not specified.
The family said it may pursue legal remedies if irregularities are established. Madagascar Tribune reported that judicial authorities had not responded to the family’s statement.

mg.headline: Madagascar's finance minister urges stronger university research support
mg.dek: At the University of Antananarivo's 65th anniversary ceremony, he cited renewable energy and called for research to shape development projects.
paragraphs: Madagascar's economy and finance minister, Herinjatovo Aimé Ramiarison, called for more support for scientific research at the University of Antananarivo in Ankatso, as the university closed celebrations of its 65th anniversary. He urged that research be used more in the country's development projects.

Ramiarison pointed to renewable energy and the Africa-wide Accelerating Sustainable Energy Transition programme, known as ASCENT, as areas where research could contribute. He also called for stronger action against corruption in the university environment to protect the credibility of higher education.
He praised local students' skills and paid tribute to teachers and educators for training future generations.

mw.headline: Blantyre-area water customers pay extra during supply cuts
mw.dek: Chatha resident Elizabeth Tembo says interruptions leave her buying bottled water and paying workers to fetch borehole water, on top of her monthly bills.
paragraphs: Residents of Chatha, on the outskirts of Blantyre City, say piped water is often cut despite monthly bills. Elizabeth Tembo, a single mother of two, said the service providers give a month rarely passes without interruptions, and that she is often told pipes have been vandalised or burst, or that power blackouts have stopped pumping.

Tembo said that when supply fails she buys five-litre bottles of drinking water at K4 000 to K6 000 from supermarkets, roughly K40 000 a week if she buys bottled water all week. She uses a community borehole when she has no money, paying part-time workers K700 to K1 000 per bucket, and says the borehole water sometimes upsets her stomach.

The Consumers Association of Malawi's executive director, John Kapito, described the constant disruptions faced by customers who pay for piped water as appalling. Water for People data cited in the report shows only 18% of Malawians have access to safely managed drinking water services.

mw.headline: Nurse takes newborn home for oxygen after Malawi clinic loses power
mw.dek: The baby was stabilised at the nurse’s home and referred to Mitundu Community Hospital, while the clinic’s outage has lasted about two and a half months.
paragraphs: A nurse at Dickson Health Centre in Lilongwe took a newborn to his home for oxygen after the baby was born in critical condition at 1:28am on November 27 and the clinic had no electricity. Nurse Tonex Mkwezalamba said the baby’s Apgar score was 3 out of 10 at birth and rose to 5 after resuscitation.

The facility’s power had been off for about two and a half months following an electrical fault, and ambulance contacts were unreachable, according to information from Mkwezalamba. Security officer Thomas Kavalo helped carry an oxygen concentrator to the nurse’s home, where the baby stabilised. By Saturday morning, the newborn was referred to Mitundu Community Hospital for further care.

Mkwezalamba said the health centre also lacks a newborn weighing scale and protective equipment, including gloves. He wants the electricity fault fixed, saying many of the facility’s services depend on power.

paragraphs: Malawi's revenue authority has suspended officer Jonathan Sulumba while it investigates a sexual misconduct complaint from a woman visiting its Lilongwe office on November 24, 2026. The woman, who is from Ireland, was seeking a certificate when she alleged she was sexually abused.

The woman described the experience as upsetting and reported it to the station manager. In a statement issued Friday evening, signed by Head of Corporate Affairs Wilma Chalulu, the authority said it was committed to establishing the facts and circumstances of the incident.

mw.headline: Malawi U-17 players complain about camp food and living conditions
mw.dek: Members of the boys' and girls' squads said the diet and conditions in their Lilongwe camp at times made them feel dehumanised.
paragraphs: Malawi's Under-17 boys' and girls' national teams have complained about the diet and living conditions at their camp in Lilongwe, days before they are due to leave for the 2026 African Union Sports Council Region 5 Youth Games in Maputo, Mozambique.

Players said that at times they feel dehumanised. The complaints did not come up in official remarks made during a visit on Thursday by the Malawi National Council of Sports and the Football Association of Malawi (FAM), and neither body has yet responded to them.
The Games begin the following week. Sports Council board chairperson Jim Kalua urged the players to believe in themselves and give their best, and praised FAM for coming to motivate the squads.

ml.headline: Mali grants Roscan Gold Mali a 12-year gold mining permit
ml.dek: The permit covers Kandiolé-Nord in Kayes region, where exploration found a deposit that can be mined economically on a large scale.
paragraphs: Mali's Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree granting Roscan Gold Mali SARL a large-scale gold mining permit at Kandiolé-Nord, in the Kéniéba district of Kayes region. The permit lasts a maximum of 12 years.

The company applied for the exploitation permit after intensive exploration identified a deposit that can be economically exploited as a large mine. The exploration permit merged an earlier Kandiolé-Nord licence with the Mankounké licence, which Quani-Or SARL transferred to the company.
The decree was issued under the mining code and the law on local content in the mining sector.

ml.headline: Mali eye hospital treats more than 300 displaced people for cataracts
ml.dek: The Bamako hospital also received specialist equipment worth more than CFA250 million, funded by Spain through its development agency and a foundation partner.
paragraphs: The University Hospital of the Institute of Tropical Ophthalmology of Africa (CHU-IOTA) in Bamako has operated on more than 300 internally displaced people with cataracts, against an initial target of 500 patients, health officials and technical partners said at a ceremony on Thursday 26 November 2026.

The ceremony, chaired by Abdoulaye Guindo, secretary general of the Ministry of Health and Social Development, was attended by the hospital's director general, Adama Issaka Guindo. Support came from Spain's development agency, the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID), and the Les Yeux du Monde Foundation, a partner since 2008. The equipment, valued above CFA250 million, includes 8 000 surgical kits, a 90 kVA standalone solar system, 10 slit lamps and an anaesthesia ventilator with a multiparameter monitor.

Spain mobilised one million euros in total, and the partnership trained around 15 practitioners. Public health specialists quoted in the report say the free procedures for the most disadvantaged patients integrate displaced people into the wider health system.

ml.headline: Bamako photography biennale opens across the capital
ml.dek: The official selection brings together 49 artists, including 25 women and six Malians, with exhibitions scheduled through 26 January 2027.
paragraphs: The fifteenth African Photography Biennale opened on Thursday at Mali’s National Museum, with works also being shown at venues across Bamako. The Rencontres de Bamako selection features 49 artists, including 25 women and six Malians, under the theme “Refabulation(s).”

The programme lists the African House of Photography, the Amadou Hampâté Bâ Cultural Palace, the Balla Fasséké Kouyaté Conservatory, the Modibo Keïta Memorial and Blonba among its sites. Galleries, restaurants and public spaces are also hosting events in the parallel programme, according to Journal du Mali.

Organisers have scheduled a professional week through 2 December, while exhibitions are due to remain open through 26 January 2027. Culture Minister Mamou Daffé paid tribute to photographers Seydou Keïta, Malick Sidibé and Sakaly at the opening ceremony.

mr.headline: Mauritania raises pensions and public-sector pay from January
mr.dek: The changes include a monthly 10 000 old-ouguiya supplement for all civilian and military retirees, with a minimum pension of 50 000.
paragraphs: President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani announced pension and salary increases in Mauritania for civil servants, military personnel and other public workers during the country’s independence anniversary. The pension reform takes effect on 1 January 2027, alongside a monthly supplement of 10 000 old ouguiyas for all civilian and military retirees.

Retirees whose pensions remain below 50 000 old ouguiyas after the supplement will receive an additional increase, taking the minimum pension to 50 000. Workers in education and training, health, the armed forces and security services will also receive salary increases, as will public employees not covered by those measures.

The announced increases include 10 000 old ouguiyas for education and health workers, 15 000 for armed forces and security personnel, and 5 000 more for paramedical staff’s risk allowance. Education workers will also receive an extra 10 000 old ouguiyas in chalk allowance.

mr.headline: Flaash Taxi lets Nouakchott riders see fares before booking
mr.dek: Launched in September, the app detects a rider’s location and lets passengers pay in cash or from their Flaash account.
paragraphs: Flaash Taxi, a ride-booking app developed by 23-year-old Mauritanian entrepreneur Mohamed Ali Camara and an associate, launched in Nouakchott in September 2026. Passengers enter a destination while the app detects their location, then select from saved landmarks to arrange a pickup.

The app displays the fare before a passenger confirms a ride and allows advance bookings, according to Le Calame. Riders can pay in cash or use their Flaash account balance. Camara said drivers’ identities and vehicle documents are checked before they are allowed to work; passengers can view a driver’s name, photo and car registration number before boarding.
Drivers can register by phone, but their documents are reviewed before approval. The app is available in French and Arabic, and users choose a language when they first open it.

mr.headline: Mauritania joins OECD Development Centre
mr.dek: The membership was formalised at a high-level meeting in Paris as the government cited dialogue on development and international experience.
paragraphs: Mauritania joined the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Development Centre on Thursday, with the membership formalised at a high-level meeting of the centre’s governing board in Paris.

Economic and Development Minister Mohamed Ahmedou M’Haimid said the move reflected Mauritania’s wish to strengthen dialogue on development and draw on international experience while respecting national priorities. He also pointed to the country’s mineral, fisheries and natural-gas resources, and its potential in renewable energy and green hydrogen.

mr.headline: Mauritania allocated 305 million francs for independence celebrations
mr.dek: A 1960 budget law drew on French aid and cancelled credits for government departments to finance the celebrations.
paragraphs: Mauritania’s 1960 budget law allocated 305 million francs to celebrations of the proclamation of independence, according to a law published in the official gazette on 7 December 1960. The measure opened 323 million francs in additional operating credits, with more than 94% assigned to a single celebrations budget line.

The law, approved by the National Assembly and promulgated by Prime Minister Mokhtar Ould Daddah, said 125 million francs came from a French grant. The government raised the rest from its own resources, including 129 million francs in cancelled credits from departments such as agriculture, justice, police and the presidency.

The remaining additional credits included 15 million francs for shared material costs, 11 million for air transport and 4 million for building rentals. The document does not break down the celebrations allocation or state how much was ultimately spent.
