mr.headline: Atar stages 5-kilometre cycling race for Independence anniversary
mr.dek: 20 cyclists raced 5 kilometres in Atar on Friday, with the five leading finishers awarded prizes.
paragraphs: A 5-kilometre cycling race started in Atar on Friday as part of events marking the 66th anniversary of Mauritania's Independence Day. Abdallahi Ould Mohamed Mahmoud, the governor of Adrar region, presided over the start.

20 cyclists took part, and the five leading finishers were crowned. Organisers also honoured the late cyclist Al-Maghfari Ould Salem Ould Bilal for his contribution to the sport. The race was organised by the Atar City Renaissance Association and Atar municipality, with the Mauritanian Olympic Committee and the national cycling federation.

The governor said Atar residents had long used bicycles in daily life and that the event would help preserve the city's local heritage. Mayor Ibrahim Ould Abdebbah said it was part of efforts to protect local culture in the region.

mu.headline: Mauritius unions challenge 4.7% inflation rate in 2027 wage talks
mu.dek: Workers’ representatives say the 2026 figure understates living costs as tripartite consultations on salary compensation get under way.
paragraphs: Mauritius unions challenged Statistics Mauritius’ 4.7% inflation estimate for 2026 at the opening of 2027 wage-compensation consultations in Port Louis on 27 November. The meeting at Victoria House brought together worker and employer representatives under Labour Minister Reza Uteem.

Union representative Atma Shanto said the movement’s members considered inflation higher than the official figure. October data showed average inflation of 4.3% over 12 months and a 6.4% year-on-year rise. Food prices increased 5.5% over a year, while fuel prices rose 17.5%.

mu.headline: Mauritius approves 124-point blue economy strategy for 2026-2035
mu.dek: The Cabinet approved a decade-long plan covering ocean-linked industries, with a new council to coordinate its implementation across government.
paragraphs: Mauritius’s Cabinet approved the Mauritius Blue Economy Strategy 2026-2035 on 27 November 2026, setting a decade-long framework for ocean-linked economic activity. The plan contains 124 recommendations and an action programme covering the next 10 years.

The strategy identifies five connected sectors and sets out priority activities, expected results, implementation schedules, responsible institutions and performance indicators. A National Blue Economy Council will oversee the strategy and coordinate work across government, according to Ion News.

The council is to include ministers responsible for the environment, tourism, financial services and economic planning, energy and public utilities, and higher education, science and research. It will also include fishing and seafarers’ associations, among other public bodies.

mz.headline: Chapo seeks Paris visit as Macron's term nears its end
mz.dek: Three dates have been proposed for a Mozambique-France meeting, but Maputo has struggled to fit them in its schedule.
paragraphs: Mozambican President Daniel Chapo has not yet made an official visit to Paris, and Africa Intelligence reports he is growing impatient over difficulties arranging one before French President Emmanuel Macron leaves office. Zitamar News understands that three dates have been proposed, but they have proved hard to accommodate on the Mozambican side.

The talks would cover a dispute over about $4.5 billion in additional costs that TotalEnergies has claimed after the suspension of Mozambique LNG in 2021. The Mozambican government has resisted the company's demands, and France is one of the country's most important investment partners, principally through TotalEnergies, which leads the $25 billion-plus project in Cabo Delgado.

Africa Intelligence suggests Macron's intervention could ease tensions between Chapo and TotalEnergies chief executive Patrick Pouyanné. Zitamar News notes that the dispute is fundamentally commercial, and a presidential meeting would not guarantee a resolution. The two countries also share interests in maritime security, counterterrorism and stability in the Mozambique Channel.

paragraphs: Namibia's financial regulator has signed testing agreements with CrowdConnect Financial Services and Bellatrix Investment Managers to pilot crowdfunding and peer-to-peer lending platforms. The agreements were signed on 24 November, placing the firms in the second cohort of the Namibia Financial Institutions Supervisory Authority (NAMFISA), the regulator's Regulatory Sandbox, which lets financial products be tested under its supervision.

Namibia has no dedicated rules for either financing model. The regulator said results from the pilots would inform a framework covering both, with attention to investor protection and financial inclusion.

na.headline: FNB Namibia urges stronger digital safeguards as 72% of transactions go online
na.dek: The bank says more than 92% of its customers are digitally enabled, and an industry writer warns that fraudsters are exploiting that convenience.
paragraphs: FNB Namibia says more than 72% of its financial transactions now take place through digital channels, and more than 92% of its customers are digitally enabled. In an article for The Brief, the bank's Amoré Nicholson argues that security must be designed around how people now use digital services.

Nicholson says fraudsters phone customers posing as their bank and use urgent warnings about missing money to pressure them into hurried decisions. Artificial intelligence (AI), which can reproduce voices and write convincing messages, makes traditional checks such as spotting spelling mistakes less reliable.

The article cites INTERPOL, the international police organisation, whose African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026 says AI enables 55% of reported cybercrime across Africa. INTERPOL's 2026 Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment estimates AI-assisted fraud is 4.5 times more profitable than conventional methods.

na.headline: Oceana reports 29% decline in Namibia horse mackerel catch
na.dek: The company attributed the drop mainly to extended vessel surveys and late-year quota shortages that reduced fishing time.
paragraphs: Oceana Group reported a 29% decline in horse mackerel catch and production in Namibia for the year ended 30 September, in its audited results. Extended planned surveys of both vessels in the second half and late-year quota shortages reduced fishing time, the company said.

Catch rates fell marginally, while unit catch costs rose by 5% as lower volumes and higher fuel costs on the unhedged portion increased expenses. Horse mackerel sales volumes stayed largely unchanged at 42 216 tons, compared with 42 768 tons in 2025. Strong demand for affordable protein, particularly smaller-sized fish, supported higher selling prices and drove profitability, Oceana said.

Average Rand selling prices increased by 18%, despite a 9% appreciation in the Rand against the US dollar. Across the group, revenue decreased 4.2% to R9.6 billion, while profit after tax rose 38.5% to R1,3 billion.
na.body:
Oceana Group reported a 29% decline in horse mackerel catch and production in Namibia for the year ended 30 September, in its audited results. Extended planned surveys of both vessels in the second half and late-year quota shortages reduced fishing time, the company said.

Catch rates fell marginally, while unit catch costs rose by 5% as lower volumes and higher fuel costs on the unhedged portion increased expenses. Horse mackerel sales volumes stayed largely unchanged at 42 216 tons, compared with 42 768 tons in 2025. Strong demand for affordable protein, particularly smaller-sized fish, supported higher selling prices and drove profitability, Oceana said.

Average Rand selling prices increased by 18%, despite a 9% appreciation in the Rand against the US dollar. Across the group, revenue decreased 4.2% to R9.6 billion, while profit after tax rose 38.5% to R1,3 billion.

na.headline: Namibia delays national airline launch to June 2027
na.dek: The Ministry of Works and Transport says aircraft delivery delays have moved the planned start of commercial flights from December 2026.
paragraphs: Namibia’s Ministry of Works and Transport has postponed the launch of national airline Namibia Air by six months, moving the planned start of commercial operations from December 2026 to June 2027. The ministry announced the change in a public notice on Friday, citing global supply and delivery timelines for the aircraft selected for the fleet.

The ministry said the new schedule reflects the earliest dates the planes can reach Namibia. Regulators must inspect the aircraft before granting an Air Operator Certificate, the approval required for the airline to fly. The ministry said the fleet must also be present for crew training, maintenance checks and ground-handling simulations.

The delay also holds up safety and compliance work by aviation authorities and airline staff. In 2025, Transport Minister Veikko Nekundi said Namibia Air would be a new carrier, not a revival of the defunct Air Namibia. Cabinet endorsed incorporating Swapo’s 2024 election-manifesto plan for a national airline into government policy in February 2026.

na.headline: Headspring gets approval for Stampriet uranium research boreholes
na.dek: The company says it will use no chemical reagents in the research phase and plans to submit a revised pilot-testing application.
paragraphs: Headspring Investments said on 3 November it had received authorisation to drill additional research boreholes for its proposed Wings Uranium Project in Namibia’s Stampriet Artesian Basin.

The company says the research phase will use no chemical reagents, but the authorisation does not permit chemical leaching or establish that the mining method is safe for groundwater. The Stampriet Aquifer Uranium Mining Association (Sauma), which is calling for clarity, wants details of what was approved, the conditions attached and the evidence supporting it.

Headspring says it will submit a revised application for pilot testing. Communities in south-eastern Namibia rely on the basin for drinking water, livestock and agriculture, with alternatives extremely limited; the aquifer system is shared with Botswana and South Africa.

ne.headline: Niger transport director warns Tahoua carriers of firm rule enforcement
ne.dek: At a meeting on Friday, Oumarou Ibrahim urged freight and fuel operators to curb overloading and keep vehicles, papers and drivers compliant.
paragraphs: Niger’s regional transport director for Tahoua, Oumarou Ibrahim, told freight and petroleum-product carriers on Friday, 27 November, that authorities would enforce transport rules firmly. The meeting at the regional goods-transport union’s headquarters addressed carriers’ role in the country’s general mobilisation.

Ibrahim called on operators to keep vehicles, documents and drivers compliant, stop overloading and improve safety when moving petroleum products. He said trucks and tankers carry goods and fuel that keep Tahoua functioning, and offered support from the regional directorate alongside enforcement.

Nazirou Boubé, national secretary-general of the Nigerien federation of goods and petroleum-product carriers, said the meeting was part of a regional awareness tour. He said the general mobilisation was decreed by President Abdourahamane Tiani on 26 December 2025 to strengthen national security, and urged drivers to follow authorities’ instructions and report anything suspicious.

ne.headline: Niger opens 100-place centre for children facing family difficulties
ne.dek: The Niamey facility, built with the NGO International Humanitarian Relief Foundation (IHH), includes classrooms, dormitories and a medical and social services building.
paragraphs: Niger opened a 100-place centre for children facing family difficulties in Niamey on Friday, 27 November. Population Minister Sidikou Ramatou Djermakoye Seyni presided at the opening, held in partnership with the NGO International Humanitarian Relief Foundation (IHH) at the Village of Francophonie.

The minister said children at the centre would receive healthy food, health care, education and care. A multidisciplinary team will supervise them day and night and seek family reintegration when needed, she said. The site includes classrooms, dormitories, a medical and social services building, play areas, a kitchen and a Friday mosque.
The minister thanked IHH and Türkiye's ambassador to Niger, Ozgur Arslan, for support in bringing the project to completion.

rw.headline: Rwanda approves investment deal for Rwamagana beverage plant
rw.dek: The Cabinet-approved agreement covers a proposed beverage manufacturing facility in Rwamagana Industrial Park, alongside plans for mobile number portability.
paragraphs: Rwanda's Cabinet approved an investment agreement with BRALIRWA Plc, a beverage maker, to establish a beverage manufacturing plant in Rwamagana Industrial Park. President Paul Kagame chaired the meeting at Village Urugwiro on November 26, 2026.

The plant is one of several projects endorsed by Cabinet. The meeting also approved an agreement with EH Venture Capital Rwanda Limited to develop Phase II of Kigali Financial Square, and a deal with SteelRwa Industries Ltd for a steel plant and expanded steel operations.

Cabinet also approved a framework for mobile number portability, letting subscribers change network operators without losing their phone numbers. The plan is intended to support transfers of mobile money accounts and related services, and to strengthen competition and service delivery.

rw.headline: Rwanda stays away as Central African bloc's leaders meet in Malabo
rw.dek: The summit is discussing the bloc's Vision 2050 plan, its 2026–2030 strategy and how it will be financed, while Rwanda is not attending.
paragraphs: Leaders of the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS), a regional bloc of 11 members, are meeting in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, for its 27th Heads of State and Government Summit. Rwanda, which should hold the bloc's rotating presidency, is not attending.

Organisers say the agenda covers Vision 2050, the 2026–2030 strategic plan and its financing, along with energy, health, maritime security and border governance. Equatorial Guinea's President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo is chairing closed-door discussions on Friday. Rwanda announced its withdrawal from the bloc in June 2025, blaming sabotage by the Democratic Republic of the Congo's government in Kinshasa.

Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi is expected to use the summit to call for full implementation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2773, which the presidency says requires Rwanda to stop supporting the AFC (Alliance Fleuve Congo), the armed group also known as M23.

rw.headline: Rwanda receives 106 citizens returning from DRC
rw.dek: The group of 28 women and 78 children crossed at Rusizi I and will receive basic assistance and civic education.
paragraphs: Rwanda received 106 citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the Rusizi I border crossing on Thursday, November 26. The group included 28 women and 78 children, with no men; they had been living in forests in the DRC.

Rusizi District Mayor Sindayiheba Phanuel said local authorities would support the returnees’ reintegration. He said children who missed school while in the forests would be helped to access education and other essential services. The group was transferred to the Nyarushishi Temporary Reception Centre in Nkungu Sector, Rusizi District.

The returnees are expected to spend three weeks there receiving basic assistance and civic education. They will complete documentation procedures before reuniting with relatives and families they left behind when they fled to the DRC.

st.headline: Água Grande clears drainage channels and starts door-to-door collection
st.dek: The district council used military and paramilitary support to remove several tonnes of waste as the rainy season approaches.
paragraphs: The Água Grande district council cleared drainage ditches in peripheral neighbourhoods of São Tomé with help from military and paramilitary forces, removing several tonnes of waste. The operation was intended to improve sanitation and reduce flood risks during the rainy season.

Councillor Claudino Soares said blocked ditches leave entire communities facing floods when it rains. Resident Cipriana Fernandes said people dump rubbish and dead animals, including dogs, pigs and chickens, into the channels. Another resident, Julião da Mata, said accumulated waste encourages mosquitoes and contributes to more malaria cases.
The council said it began door-to-door waste collection across the district about 15 days ago, with daily collection in all localities, according to councillor Abdelazy do Rosário.

st.headline: Príncipe swears in Nascimento's five-secretary regional government
st.dek: Prime Minister Américo Ramos pledged central-government support as the new administration takes office after winning six of nine regional seats.
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe's Prime Minister Américo Ramos swore in the new regional government of Príncipe on Friday, 27 November, with Filipe Nascimento as its president and five regional secretaries. Ramos said the central government would provide the support needed for the island to grow, with more opportunities, more jobs, better infrastructure and the protection of its natural heritage.

Nascimento said his administration would open a new cycle of progress and transformation for Príncipe, based on a change of mindset and greater demands at work. He said the regional government was counting on the Republic's government and defended a responsible, constructive and solidary autonomy. He pledged greater transparency and strict management of public resources, saying the government wanted action and rigour rather than promises.

Nascimento's UMPP, the Unidade Mais Pela Pátria party, won six of the nine regional seats in the 27 September election, while the Movimento Verde, led by Nestor Umbelina, took three. The five secretaries cover finance and economic coordination, infrastructure, environment and land use, education, culture and sport, health, equality and social protection, and agriculture, fisheries and trade.

st.headline: Tela Non account says Lucas remains jailed after 2022 military incident

paragraphs: Tela Non reported that Lucas, an artist and family head, remains imprisoned after an incident involving soldiers in São Tomé on 24 November 2022. He was at a kiosk near the central Dr Ayres de Menezes hospital after work, the account says.

Lucas said he had gone there after an argument with his wife. Virgílio Pontes, then a colonel, struck Rodrigues’s hand, diverting the shot into a wall, the account says.
Pontes later became chief of the armed forces’ general staff, according to Tela Non. The report gives no court ruling or official response.

st.headline: São Tomé and Príncipe sends swimmer to world championships in Beijing
st.dek: World Aquatics invited the country to compete from 1 to 6 December, after a two-year project built local swimming capacity.
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe will compete at the World Swimming Championships in Beijing from 1 to 6 December 2026, following an invitation from World Aquatics, the sport’s international governing body.

The São Tomé and Príncipe Swimming Federation said the entry followed two years of work by its “São Tomé and Príncipe Swimming” project with Portugal’s Association of Swimming Coaches. The project trained coaches, supported a local club and swimming school, and gave swimmers international competition opportunities. José Dias, a swimming teacher and swimmer trained in São Tomé and Príncipe, prepared in Portugal during October with several clubs.
The federation’s president, Angélico dos Santos, said the participation involved local and international partners, volunteers and coaches. The championships run through 6 December.

sn.headline: Sonko urges Senegal’s president to dissolve Parliament from 2 December
sn.dek: The former prime minister says Bassirou Diomaye Faye can dissolve the legislature once the constitutional date arrives.
paragraphs: Ousmane Sonko, Senegal’s former prime minister and leader of the parliamentary majority party, urged President Bassirou Diomaye Faye to dissolve Parliament in an address posted to social media on the evening of Thursday, 26 November. The Constitution allows dissolution from 2 December.

Sonko’s call comes during a dispute between the legislature and executive that has been under way since June, according to RFI Afrique. The president has not been reported as responding to the appeal.

Separately, the National Assembly’s bureau, chaired by Sonko on Friday, 27 November, adopted four proposals to create parliamentary inquiry commissions. The inquiries will cover debt, Banco Santander and special funds.

sn.headline: Senegal’s anti-corruption body targets 50% score with Forum Civil
sn.dek: The partners are beginning a self-assessment after Senegal remained in the red zone of Transparency International’s corruption index since 1998.
paragraphs: Senegal’s National Office for the Fight Against Fraud and Corruption (OFNAC) and civil society group Forum Civil held a workshop in Saly on November 27 and 28 to develop steps to improve the country’s score on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index. OFNAC president Moustapha Ka said the partners aim to reach 50%, which he described as the threshold for leaving the index’s red zone.

Ka said the workshop follows a partnership agreement with Forum Civil and is intended to start a national self-assessment rather than leave Senegal to respond only to international rankings. He said corruption is present across public administrations, including the justice system, but OFNAC has no precise figures to rank the most vulnerable sectors.

OFNAC has begun studies with the environment and transport ministries and held a meeting with the justice ministry in Saly the previous week. Ka said reaching the 50% target requires efforts beyond his office.

sn.headline: Casamance women’s peace platform urges inquiry into Oulampane mayor attack
sn.dek: The group called for calm and said authorities must establish responsibility after the mayor was seriously burned while asleep on 26 November.
paragraphs: The Platform of Women for Peace in Casamance has called on Senegalese authorities to investigate an attack that seriously burned the mayor of Oulampane, in the Ziguinchor region, while he slept on the night of 26 November. The organisation issued its statement on 27 November.

The platform condemned the violence without regard to the attacker’s identity or motives, and urged residents to remain calm while administrative and judicial authorities and security forces investigate. Le Soleil reported that the mayor was taken to Ziguinchor and admitted to intensive care at the Peace Hospital; his condition was stable, according to the outlet.

The group said defending women’s rights should not excuse violence committed by women, during the 16 days of activism against gender-based violence. It urged families and communities to use dialogue and mediation to resolve disputes.

sn.headline: Senegal deploys more than 3 500 personnel for eastern security exercise
sn.dek: Boundou 2026 runs in Tambacounda and Kédougou from 28 November to 6 December, with free medical consultations also planned in some localities.
paragraphs: Senegal’s armed forces are holding Boundou 2026, a national exercise involving more than 3 500 military and paramilitary personnel in the eastern regions of Tambacounda and Kédougou from 28 November to 6 December 2026.

The exercise brings together the military, gendarmerie, police, firefighters, customs, prison administration and environment services to assess and strengthen coordination between units, according to the armed forces’ information and public relations directorate. The army health service plans free consultations for residents of some localities in the exercise area.

A press briefing by the army chief of staff is scheduled for 10 a.m. on Monday, 30 November, at the Mamadou Lamine Dramé military camp in Tambacounda. A VIP day is planned in Goudiry on the morning of 4 December.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone passes 2027 finance bill with tax changes
sl.dek: The amended bill sets out revenue measures including a Le10 annual poll tax and a 20% surcharge on qualifying imported goods.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone’s Parliament passed the Finance Bill 2027 with amendments on Thursday, November 26, after debate between ruling and opposition lawmakers. The bill provides the legal framework for the government’s revenue and tax proposals for the 2027 financial year.

Finance Minister Karefa Ansumana Francis Kargbo said the proposals include changes to income tax and customs laws, closer monitoring of tax exemptions, electronic tax administration and a poll tax for residents aged 18 and above. The annual charge is Le10 within local council jurisdictions; indigent people, full-time students and people with severe disabilities would be exempt. The bill also proposes a 20% surcharge on imported goods already produced locally in sufficient quantities and to acceptable quality standards.

Lawmakers raised concerns about revenue shortfalls, tax waivers, customs delays and consultation on local taxes. The legislation also proposes linking bank accounts to taxpayer or national identification numbers and adjusting non-taxable income thresholds to the statutory minimum wage.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone regulator reports NLE 7.4 million in 2024 revenue
sl.dek: The electricity and water commission said revenue from levies and licenses rose from NLE 2.3 million in 2023.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's Electricity and Water Regulatory Commission (SLEWRC), which regulates electricity and water providers, recorded NLE 7.4 million in internal revenue from levies and licenses in 2024, up from NLE 2.3 million in 2023. NLE stands for New Leone, the country's currency.

Deputy Director Sama Sandi told Ministry of Finance budget discussions on 21 August 2024 that the commission received nothing from the ministry in 2023, despite NLE 954 thousand being designated against NLE 2.037 million budgeted for recurrent spending. In 2024 it again received nothing, after NLE 911 thousand was allocated. Sandi said the commission resolved an average of 80% of complaints within a week and took enforcement action against 64 water companies it described as non-compliant.
For 2025 to 2027, Sandi submitted a budget of NLE 5,590.29. The commission's plans include completing a tariff model for solar mini-grids and monitoring electricity and water rates.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone Parliament receives five public-service audit reports
sl.dek: The reports, dated August 2026, examine building permits, maternal health, emergency care, electricity generation, education and waste management.
paragraphs: Sierra Leone’s Parliament received five audit reports on Thursday, November 26, covering public services and institutions, including healthcare, electricity generation and education. Deputy Speaker Ibrahim Tawa Conteh, who chairs Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee, tabled the reports in the presence of Auditor-General Abdul Aziz and Audit Service Sierra Leone officials.

The audits examine delays in building permits in the Western Area, the Free Health Care Initiative’s role in reducing maternal mortality, and emergency-care response there. Other reports assess electricity generation by the state electricity company and independent power producers, and service delivery in education and solid waste management in selected district councils.
All five reports are dated August 2026. They were presented for parliamentary scrutiny of the performance of ministries, agencies and local councils.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal trade sustains livelihoods as tree loss threatens food security
sl.dek: A 65-year-old burner says his family depends on the trade, while the Environmental Protection Agency warns that producers are cutting fruit trees.
paragraphs: Charcoal production supports livelihoods in Sierra Leone, where 65-year-old Pa Alimamy says he has burned charcoal for more than two decades to keep himself and his family alive. The trade is common in Freetown and other regional headquarters, as households seek cooking fuel they can afford.

Paul Lamin, the Environmental Protection Agency’s director of natural resource governance, said burners are cutting economic trees such as orange and mango, leaving land bare and threatening food security. He said trees take a long time to grow back, and acknowledged that people have few alternative energy options. The government’s National Energy Compact says 36% of the population has electricity access and clean cooking access is 15%.

The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates traditional wood energy produces 1/2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, equal to 2-7% of global human-caused greenhouse gas emissions; sub-Saharan Africa accounts for one third of emissions from wood energy. The agency warns that continued unsustainable production and use could harm forests and future wood-energy supplies.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone's vice presidency has never produced an elected president
sl.dek: A February analysis by public policy analyst Foday M. Daboh says the office has often left its holders without an independent political base or a path to succession.
paragraphs: No vice president in Sierra Leone has ever been elected president, according to a February analysis by Foday M. Daboh, a public policy analyst and political economist. Daboh argues the current vice president may already face the same barrier, though the article does not name the incumbent.

He says governments have used the office to balance regional, religious and ethnic interests, appease party blocs, neutralise rivals and reward loyalty. That has left many vice presidents without an independent political base or a clear succession route. Solomon Ekuma Berewa, vice president under the Kabbah government, lost the 2007 presidential election as the SLPP candidate to Ernest Bai Koroma.

Daboh also cites Sam-Sumana, who was expelled from the APC after falling out with the president, and Francis Minah, executed after an alleged failed coup in 1987. He notes that the 1991 Constitution envisages the vice presidency as a stabilising institution.

so.headline: Five Somali Supreme Court judges refuse order to resume duties
so.dek: They say armed forces still control the court and that their personal protection has not been restored since the Nov. 5 rulings.
paragraphs: Five Somali Supreme Court judges have refused an order to resume work, telling Chief Justice Ibrahim Idle Suleiman that a Nov. 25 deadline had no legal basis. They say security forces still occupy the court building in Mogadishu and their personal protection has been withdrawn.

In their letter, the judges said they had not abandoned their posts and could not work independently amid threats, surveillance and restrictions on movement. The Nov. 5 rulings found President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term extension unlawful and the dismissal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed invalid. The judges demanded the forces leave, their protection be restored and the decisions be enforced.

The presidency rejected the rulings, and the state attorney general said they had no legal effect. On Nov. 18, six judges, including the five who signed the term-extension ruling, challenged the government’s actions at the East African Court of Justice in Arusha.

so.headline: Somalia leaves transport minister’s armed confrontation unanswered
so.dek: A video showed State Minister Abdikarim Abdow Hayder carrying an AK-47 to the ministry gates amid a dispute over vehicle number-plate kickbacks.
paragraphs: A video circulated on Thursday showed Somalia’s State Minister of Transport Abdikarim Abdow Hayder carrying an AK-47 and wearing a tactical vest as he approached the Ministry of Transport and Civil Aviation in Mogadishu. Witnesses and journalists described it as an attempt to confront and kill Transport Minister Mohamed Farah Nuh.

Media reports linked the confrontation to a dispute over how the officials divided proceeds from vehicle number plates; Hayder reportedly believed he had been denied his share. More than 72 hours after the video appeared, the government had neither arrested nor dismissed him.

Days earlier, the civil aviation agency accused Nuh of entering its offices with armed troops and raised safety concerns. The ministry’s director general had also entered the minister’s office carrying an AK-47 during an earlier dispute, the report said.

ss.headline: UN food agencies rank South Sudan among five worst global hunger hotspots
ss.dek: Warning of rising risk, the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme placed the country in their highest-concern group.
paragraphs: South Sudan has been placed among the world's five hunger hotspots of highest concern by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP), in their latest Hunger Hotspots report.

Both agencies say severe food insecurity is becoming more likely there, pointing to fighting, falling humanitarian funding and climate-linked shocks. The available account gives no separate figure for how many people are hungry.
The report names five hotspots worldwide, but the available account does not identify the other four.

ss.headline: South Sudan youth groups press for 20% representation in government
ss.dek: An assessment found little improvement from last year, while the country has no legislature in place for a new parliamentary count.
paragraphs: Youth-led organisations in South Sudan called on Friday for greater representation in government, saying young people remain underrepresented in leadership and decision-making. Florence Agiba, executive director of youth organisation Markaz Al-Salam, said a recent assessment found little improvement from last year, despite progress in some states.

Agiba cited Unity State, where four young people had been appointed ministers. The latest assessment excluded parliament because South Sudan has no legislature in place; in the previous assessment, young people made up about 4.81% of parliamentarians, or approximately 23 of 550 members. Markaz Al-Salam is preparing a fact sheet with support from Norwegian People’s Aid and the National Youth Union.

Agiba called for youth representation to reach at least 20%. Michael Gorjin Kuol of Norwegian People’s Aid proposed a dialogue with political parties and election bodies, while counsel Izale Benjamin said many young people do not know the National Youth Policy provides for 20% representation.

ss.headline: South Sudan urges partners to back national control of peace process
ss.dek: Foreign Affairs Minister Cecilia Adut Manyok said the African Union, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development and the UN task force should help end the transition, not.
paragraphs: South Sudan's Foreign Affairs Minister Cecilia Adut Manyok urged international partners to respect national ownership of the peace process as a joint task force began work in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Friday. Speaking for President Salva Kiir Mayardit, she said the government and South Sudanese people hold primary responsibility for peace, security, reconciliation and democratic governance.

The task force brings together the African Union (AU), the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), a regional bloc of East African states, and the United Nations. Adut said its role should be to help conclude the transitional period, which she said the country is approaching, rather than make the process indefinite. She also called for adequate financial and technical support from partners.

Adut cited resolutions from an inter-party dialogue concluded by Kiir in Juba on Thursday. They address political freedoms, campaign security, party financing and a 35% affirmative-action provision for women. The dialogue included Juba-based parties but excluded opposition groups operating abroad.

ss.headline: Abyei standards bureau destroys 795 packages of expired goods
ss.dek: The seized stock from shops at Mulmul Market included 718 flour bags, soft drinks, alcohol and jangaro.
paragraphs: South Sudan’s Bureau of Standards in the Abyei Special Administrative Area destroyed 795 packages of expired goods seized from shops in Mulmul Market, Abyei Municipality. The bureau acted over concerns about public health and safety.

Among the seized stock, officials counted 718 flour bags, 63 cartons of soft drinks, 10 cartons of alcohol and four bags of jangaro. Caretaker Mayor Bakor Mayar said the goods had expired and were poorly stored, leaving them damaged and infested with insects that could put consumers at risk.

Mayar urged residents to check expiry dates and traders to inspect stock regularly and report expired products to authorities. Caretaker Information Minister Yohona Akol said the government would remove expired and unsafe goods from local markets.

ss.headline: South Sudan sets December 12 launch for Boma-Badingilo heritage site
ss.dek: The landscape was inscribed in July as the country’s first UNESCO World Heritage Site, but is also listed as being in danger.
paragraphs: South Sudan will officially launch the Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape on December 12, five months after it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List. Julia Amon Wantok, the caretaker undersecretary at the Ministry of Culture, Museums and National Heritage, announced the date on Friday in Juba.

The launch will be organised with the Ministry of Wildlife Conservation and Tourism, UNESCO, African Parks and other partners, Amon said. The She Stand Women’s Museum will also take part. The landscape includes Boma and Badingilo national parks, wetlands, floodplains and savannahs, and is home to an estimated six million migratory antelopes.

UNESCO has also placed the site on its List of World Heritage in Danger, citing threats including poaching, insecurity and infrastructure development. The antelope species there include white-eared kob, tiang and Mongalla gazelles.

sd.headline: EU, US and partners urge Sudan's warring sides to open aid routes
sd.dek: A joint warning says 19.5 million people face acute food insecurity and calls for support for Sudan's winter planting season.
paragraphs: Pressure is mounting on Sudan's warring parties to ease limits on food aid. The EU, US, UK and more than 20 other countries, in a joint statement dated 26 October, warned that hunger is getting worse and asked the sides to lift restrictions on deliveries. Some 41% of the population, or 19.5 million people, now face acute food insecurity.

Five million of them are at emergency levels of hunger, the signatories said. They cautioned that severe acute malnutrition could reach more than 825,000 children and that areas short of food could double in number. Fighting, displacement, damaged infrastructure and broken food supply chains were named as the main causes, with aid restrictions and El Niño-linked drought adding strain.

Signatories asked the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces to guarantee safe aid access, shield humanitarian workers and end strikes on civilian infrastructure, including farms and food systems. They also called for more international money for the winter planting season and for locally led relief efforts.

sd.headline: Ramaphosa backs urgent efforts to end Sudan war
sd.dek: The South African president voiced concern over worsening humanitarian conditions after Abdullah Hamdok’s delegation presented a Sudanese-led political plan.
paragraphs: South African President Cyril Ramaphosa backed urgent efforts to end Sudan’s war during a meeting in Pretoria on Friday with a delegation led by former Sudanese prime minister Abdullah Hamdok. The delegation presented a plan from the Forces of the Declaration of Principles for ending the fighting through a Sudanese-led political process.

The group warned that rising signs of famine were worsening the humanitarian crisis and said the war threatened Sudan’s unity and regional peace and security. Ramaphosa expressed concern about conditions in Sudan and said South Africa supported efforts to secure a lasting peace.

The delegation’s visit to South Africa ran from 24 to 27 November and included meetings with government officials, among them the national security adviser and the foreign ministry’s Africa director, as well as a working session with the African Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes.

sd.headline: Admissions committee opens in-person university application centers in western Sudan
sd.dek: The offices serve students facing poor internet access, with centers in five South Darfur localities and additional sites in Darfur and Kordofan.
paragraphs: Sudan’s Higher Committee for University Admissions and Certificate Evaluation has opened in-person application centers across western Sudan for students seeking places at designated universities. The offices are intended for applicants who struggle to use online platforms because of poor internet connectivity.

Committee chairman Dr. Musa Al-Amin Hamouda told Radio Tamazuj that online applications opened nine days before the centers were announced. The committee has offices in five South Darfur localities, as well as El Geneina and For-baranga, with additional centers in Kordofan. Applicants pay a fee of 20,000 Sudanese pounds, according to prospective student Jamal Hassan, who applied at the University of El Daein.

The committee is using examination pass lists to contact eligible students, and students who sat exams in army-controlled areas but now live in western Sudan can apply in the second admissions round. Another applicant, Rashida Babiker, said she selected media studies and urged students to apply quickly because the application window is limited.

sd.headline: University of Zalingei finalizes preparations to reopen
sd.dek: The university, closed after insecurity and fighting in the city, is addressing campus security, electricity, drinking water and displaced residents.
paragraphs: The University of Zalingei in Sudan’s Central Darfur state has completed preparations to reopen and resume academic activities, its administration announced. The university has been closed following insecurity and armed confrontations in the city.

Chancellor Awadallah Al-Douma said the administration and the state government reviewed campus security and essential services, including electricity and safe drinking water. Central Darfur government Secretary-General Amer Hamdan said representatives of the State Security Committee and the Sudanese Agency for Relief and Humanitarian Operations also discussed reopening measures. He said forces operating under the Tasis Alliance had adopted the arrangements.

Hamdan said the relief agency was responsible for helping internally displaced people sheltering on campus relocate safely to designated sites in eastern Zalingei. The university still needs facility rehabilitation, restored services and safety measures for students and staff before classes resume.

sd.headline: SPLM-IO education secretary resigns and relinquishes four positions
sd.dek: Gatkuoth Lok Gatwich Diet said he would leave party politics for academic, professional and other interests outside the movement.
paragraphs: Gatkuoth Lok Gatwich Diet, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition (SPLM-IO) secretary for Education, Science and Technology, has resigned from the party, effective immediately. His resignation letter, dated November 23, also relinquished his other party roles.

In an email to Radio Tamazuj on Friday, Lok said he was leaving four positions: education secretary in the General Secretariat, secretary of the National Liberation Council Standing Committee on Education, Science and Technology, a council membership and party membership. He cited personal reasons and said he planned to pursue academic, professional and other interests outside active politics.

The SPLM-IO remains split between factions led by interim leader Regina Joseph Kaba and Oyet Nathaniel Pierino after a leadership dispute following chairman Dr. Riek Machar’s detention in Juba in March 2025. South Sudan’s general election is scheduled for February 11, 2027.

tg.headline: Togo brings 176 citizens home from Mali after departures from Guinea
tg.dek: The government received the returnees at three sites and is still identifying Togolese in Burkina Faso who want to come home.
paragraphs: Togo’s government brought 176 citizens back from Bamako, Mali, after they left Guinea amid operations against illegal gold mining. The return was organised by a mission sent to Mali and Burkina Faso to identify Togolese, assess their needs and prepare travel home, the Security Ministry said.

The returnees arrived at Dapaong, Sokodé and Logopé, where authorities arranged family reunions and registered them for biometric national identity cards. The ministry said the operation involved several government departments and the National Civil Protection Agency.

At the Bobo-Dioulasso transit centre in Burkina Faso, authorities had counted 983 Togolese among foreign nationals there as of 20 November. Togo is continuing work to identify those who want to return. Guinea’s operations against illegal gold mining began on 2 November, and Togo’s Foreign Ministry urged young people on 17 November to follow migration and mining rules.

tg.headline: Togo opposition calls for urgent search for missing priest
tg.dek: Four opposition groups, including the Manifeste Génération Togo, urged authorities to find Father Éric Ébélaki, a vicar in Kara, and return him safely.
paragraphs: Four Togolese opposition groups called on the authorities to search without delay for Father Éric Ébélaki, a vicar in Kara, whose disappearance was made public by the Conference of Bishops of Togo. The groups are the DMK-Originale, the Démocratie Maintenant pour le Progrès (DMP), the Libres Démocrates Progressistes (LDP) and the movement Touche pas à ma Constitution.

In a declaration published on 27 November, the groups said they were very concerned and asked officials to take all necessary steps to find the priest safe. The Conference of Bishops of Togo said its president, Bishop Jacques Danka Longa of Kara, had noted that the priest's absence was found on the morning of Thursday 26 November and that the competent authorities had been notified.

Radio France Internationale, citing unnamed local sources, reported that the priest had been missing since 24 November and that his room was found in disarray with the door broken. The same outlet said the room had been set on fire between May and June by unidentified people. The authorities in Lomé did not respond to its requests for comment, and no official update on the search had been reported.

tg.headline: Togo police seize 6 918 cartridges hidden in vehicle
tg.dek: The ammunition was found in a vehicle travelling from Ghana through Togo toward Nigeria, and the driver said he had made two earlier trips.
paragraphs: Togo’s national police seized 6 918 calibre 12 cartridges from a vehicle in Togo on 23 November 2026, as it travelled from Ghana toward Nigeria. Officers found the ammunition concealed in a metal compartment beneath the vehicle’s floor. Police presented the seizure to reporters in Lomé on Friday, 27 November.

The driver, O. Georges, a 30-year-old Ghanaian, told investigators his employer in Accra had given him the cargo for delivery to a partner in Lagos. He said this was his third such trip; the previous two had passed without incident. Police said the cartridges were intended for illicit trade.

The police research and investigations brigade has opened an inquiry and is seeking to identify and dismantle the wider network. Georges is due to be brought before the public prosecutor at the Lomé court after the investigation.

tn.headline: Tunisian olive growers say oil must sell for 15 dinars a litre to cover costs
tn.dek: Midani Dhaoui, head of the Tunisian farmers' union, says rising costs and falling olive prices are squeezing producers.
paragraphs: Tunisian olive growers would need to sell a litre of olive oil for 15 dinars to cover their production costs, Midani Dhaoui, president of the Tunisian farmers' union, said on Express FM on Friday, 27 November. Olives are currently sold for between 1.4 and 1.8 dinars a kilogram.

Dhaoui said the main problem is the gap between what it costs to produce olives and the price farmers receive for them. He said the current price does not adequately cover farm expenses, and he blamed the growing number of middlemen for widening the gap between producer and consumer prices.

On citrus, Dhaoui said this season's harvest is slightly below last year's but should meet export needs. Citrus now costs 1.5 dinars a kilogram to produce, and he urged growers to find new export markets abroad.

tn.headline: Solar industry body urges Tunisia to revisit rejected tax cuts
tn.dek: The photovoltaic chamber wants lawmakers to reconsider lower import duties on solar panels and exemptions for storage batteries in the 2027 finance bill.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s national photovoltaic chamber has asked the government to return two rejected tax measures to a plenary debate on the 2027 finance bill. Articles 49 and 50 would reduce customs duties on imported solar panels and exempt storage batteries from taxes.

The chamber, which belongs to the Tunisian Union of Industry, Trade and Handicrafts (UTICA), made its request after joint finance and budget committees rejected the articles on 23 November. The committees include members of the Assembly of the Representatives of the People and the National Council of Regions and Districts.
The measures concern taxes on equipment used to generate and store solar electricity. Lawmakers must decide whether the articles return for discussion in plenary.

tn.headline: Tunisia and UN sign five-year cooperation framework
tn.dek: The 2027-2031 agreement sets priorities for jobs, social inclusion and water security, aligned with Tunisia’s 2026-2030 development plan.
paragraphs: Tunisia and the United Nations signed a cooperation framework on Friday, 27 November, at the foreign ministry in Tunis, covering 2027-2031. The five-year agreement sets out work on economic and social development, job creation and sustainable resource management.

Foreign Minister Mohamed Ali Nafti and UN Resident Coordinator Rana Taha signed the framework. Its three priorities are human development and social inclusion; inclusive economic change and decent jobs; and ecological and energy transition, including water and food security. The plan calls for support to health and education services, social protection, entrepreneurship and opportunities for young people and women.

The framework is intended to guide UN programmes in line with Tunisia’s 2026-2030 development plan. Nafti called for stronger coordination among participants and more funding, and urged partner countries and donors to continue supporting Tunisia’s programmes.

tn.headline: United ATS opens Tunis aviation training centre for regional clients
tn.dek: The company says local training, priced in Tunisian dinars, can replace services that aviation customers currently buy abroad.
paragraphs: United ATS Tunisia has opened an aviation training centre in the Lac district of Tunis, aiming to serve local and regional demand for air traffic control and other specialist skills. The company says Tunisia could become a regional training hub, with potential to attract clients from African and French-speaking markets.

Sofiane Bejaoui, the centre’s chief instructor, said its courses would be offered locally at competitive costs and in Tunisian dinars, replacing services now purchased abroad. He said clients from Iraq, Libya and Kuwait already come to Tunisia, and that the country has qualified instructors and aviation professionals with international experience.

Ghofran Ben Ameur, United ATS Tunisia’s training coordinator, said shortages of qualified air navigation and air traffic control staff affect Europe, the United States and other countries. The company has also delivered technical training at international centres and for aviation businesses in Libya and Egypt.

tn.headline: Tunisia calls for roadmap to recycle construction waste in roads
tn.dek: The government says future road projects could use 20 to 30% recycled material, while a trial on the RN3 tests durability.
paragraphs: Tunisia’s equipment minister, Salah Zouari, called on Friday 27 November 2026 for a rapid roadmap to collect, sort, treat and reuse demolition and construction waste in road infrastructure. The country has nearly 14 million tonnes of this waste, according to estimates cited by the minister.

A 1.2-kilometre trial section of national road No. 3 in Ben Arous was built with recycled material and reopened to traffic on 19 October. The trial is assessing its resistance and durability under real traffic conditions, as well as whether it meets quality and safety requirements.

Prime Minister Sarra Zaâfrani Zenzri said on 9 November that future road projects could include between 20 and 30% recycled material; those proportions are to be written into specifications for the projects concerned.

zm.dek: Annual inflation edged up to 6.4% in November, while actual and projected inflation remain within the bank’s 6 to 8% target band.
paragraphs: The Bank of Zambia kept its Monetary Policy Rate at 10.75% after annual inflation rose to 6.4% in November, from 6.3% in October. The decision leaves the central bank’s benchmark unchanged as consumer-price growth increased for a second month.

Governor Denny Kalyalya said the bank’s actual and projected inflation remain within its 6 to 8% target band. The Monetary Policy Committee reached the decision after meeting on November 25 and 26 to review recent economic conditions.
The bank disclosed the decision on November 27. It did not announce a change to the rate.

zm.headline: Zambia president rejects poverty excuse for child marriage
zm.dek: Hakainde Hichilema also warned of action against adult-led "sex parties" involving minors in Lusaka.
paragraphs: President Hakainde Hichilema stated that poverty is not a valid excuse for child and early marriages, emphasizing that the government has established sufficient empowerment programmes for citizens. Speaking as the African Union Champion on Ending Child Marriage, he expressed concern over perpetrators who continue these practices despite available support.

Hichilema further announced that the government will take action against so-called "sex parties" in Lusaka, where adults allegedly engage with underage children. He described such conduct as delinquent and immoral, stating that as a parent himself, he would not tolerate seeing children involved in these activities.

The president noted receiving reports about these gatherings, reinforcing his stance that existing state programmes provide adequate tools to prevent exploitation. His remarks signal a direct challenge to communities using economic hardship to justify violations of national laws protecting minors.

eh.headline: UN mission to leave Western Sahara by 31 January without holding referendum
eh.dek: MINURSO spent 35 years without organising the vote, while helping monitor the 1991 ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front.
paragraphs: The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) is due to leave the territory by 31 January 2027 without organising the self-determination referendum in its mandate, ECS Saharaui reported. The mission was created 35 years ago to let Sahrawis decide the territory's political future.

The referendum process stalled over disputes including the voter census and identification. Morocco opposed repeated efforts to update the census drawn up during Spanish rule, the report said. MINURSO also monitored the 1991 ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front for decades.

Hostilities resumed in November 2020 after a Moroccan military intervention in the El Guerguerat area. Spanish journalist Ignacio Cembrero, who has followed the conflict for four decades, told RFI he fears a military escalation once the mission is gone.

ls.headline: Lesotho's acting state prosecutor warns sexual-offence cases strain her office
ls.dek: Lehlanako Mofilikoane says pressure from some parents on complainants to drop charges can also hinder cases reaching court.
paragraphs: Lesotho's Acting Director of Public Prosecutions, the country's acting chief state prosecutor, Advocate Lehlanako Mofilikoane, said her office is struggling to handle the sexual-offence cases reported each day. She made the remarks at a 16 Days of Activism event at Pioneer Mall in Maseru on Wednesday.

Mofilikoane said some parents press victims to withdraw charges against alleged perpetrators, which can obstruct cases reaching court. She urged communities to report offences and share information about the rights of women and children. Prosecutors, she said, would pursue gender-based violence cases without fear or favour and keep victims informed.
The campaign runs from 25 November to 10 December. Mofilikoane did not announce staffing or case-management changes.
